lines.text: The Virtuous City

Al-Farabi's Opinions of the People of the Virtuous City (Ārāʾ ahl al-madīna al-fāḍila), begun in Baghdad and finished in Damascus in 942–43: the Islamic world's answer to Plato's Republic. It climbs down from the First, through the intellects and the heavens, to matter, the human soul and the Active Intellect, prophecy and dreams, and then builds the virtuous city and its first ruler, set against the ignorant, immoral, changed and erring cities. A new translation from Friedrich Dieterici's German (Der Musterstaat, Leiden 1900), checked paragraph by paragraph against the Arabic of the Cairo edition (1906), which stands beside it; where Dieterici departs from the Arabic, the Arabic is followed. Words in square brackets are the translator's. References are to the pages of Dieterici's Arabic edition (Leiden 1895). Not yet reviewed by a scholar. I. On the First Existent
In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. This is a book composed by Abu Nasr al-Farabi on the principles of the opinions of the people of the virtuous city.

The First Existent is the First Cause of the existence of all the other existents. He is free of every kind of deficiency, while everything other than Him cannot be free of having some kind of deficiency in it, either one or more than one. But the First is free of all its kinds.

His existence, then, is the most excellent existence and the most prior existence; there can be no existence more excellent or more prior than His. In excellence of existence He is of the highest kind, and in perfection of existence He is of the loftiest rank. For this reason non-existence cannot in any way be mixed with His existence and substance.
Non-existence and the opposite occur only in what lies beneath the sphere of the Moon; and non-existence is the not-being of that whose nature is to exist.

Nor can He have existence in potentiality, in any manner at all, nor is there any possibility, in any way whatever, that He should not exist. For this reason He is eternal, everlasting in existence by His substance and His essence, without needing, in order to be eternal, anything else that would sustain His permanence; rather He is sufficient by His substance for His permanence and for the perpetuity of His existence.
Nor can there be any existence at all like His existence; nor, at the rank of His existence, is there any existence that could be His or be supplied to Him.

He is the existent for which there can be no cause through which, or from which, or for the sake of which, its existence came about. For He is not matter, nor does His subsistence lie in matter or in any substrate at all; rather His existence is free of all matter and of every substrate.

Nor does He have a form, since form can exist only in matter. If He had a form, His essence would be composed of matter and form; and if that were so, His subsistence would be through the two parts of which He is composed, and His existence would have a cause, for each of its parts is a cause of the existence of the whole. But we have laid down that He is a first cause.

Nor does His existence have a purpose and an end, such that He would exist only in order to fulfil that end and that purpose; otherwise that would be in some way a cause of His existence, and He would not be a first cause. Nor did He acquire His existence from anything else prior to Him; and He is still further from having acquired it from what is beneath Him.
II. On the Denial of a Partner to Him, Exalted Be He

He is distinct in His substance from everything other than Him, and the existence that is His cannot belong to anything else besides Him. For whatever has this existence cannot differ in any way, nor be other in any way, from another thing that also has this existence; there would then not be two, but only one single essence.

For if there were a difference between them, that by which they differ would be other than that in which they share. The thing by which each of them differs from the other would then be one part of what constitutes their existence, and that in which they share would be the other part. Each of them would then be divisible in its account, and each of its two parts would be a cause of the subsistence of its essence. It would then not be first; rather there would be another existent prior to it, which is the cause of its existence. And that is absurd.

If, on the other hand, that other were the one in which lies that by which it differs from this one, while in this one there were nothing by which it differs from that one except as a consequence of the thing by which that one differs, then the thing by which that other differs from this one must be the existence proper to that other, while the existence of this one is common to both. The existence of that other, therefore, would be composed of two things: something proper to it, and something in which it shares with this one. So the existence of that one is not the existence of this one; rather the essence of this one is simple and undivided, while the essence of that one is divided. That one, then, has two parts by which it subsists; its existence therefore has a cause, and so its existence is below the existence of this one and more deficient than it. It is not, then, of the first rank of existence.

Further, if there were, outside Him and in something else, an existence like His in species, He would not be perfect in existence. For the perfect is that outside of which no existence of the species of its existence can be found, and this holds of anything whatever. The perfect in magnitude is that outside of which no magnitude is found; the perfect in beauty is that outside of which no beauty of the species of its beauty is found; likewise the perfect in substance is that outside of which nothing of the species of its substance is found. So too with every body that is perfect: there can be nothing else of its species besides it, as with the sun, the moon, and each of the other stars. And since the First is perfect in existence, that existence cannot belong to anything else besides Him. He is therefore alone and singular in that existence; and in this respect He is one.
III. On the Denial of an Opposite to Him

Further, He cannot have an opposite. This becomes clear once it is known what “opposite” means. The opposite is distinct from the thing, so that the opposite of a thing can never be the thing itself. But not everything distinct is an opposite, nor is everything that cannot be the thing an opposite; rather the opposite is whatever, in addition, is in conflict with it, so that it is the nature of each of the two to annul and destroy the other when they come together, and the nature of each that, if it comes to exist where the other exists, it makes the other cease to exist, and is itself made to cease to exist where it is, through the existence of the other in the thing in which it had been. This holds generally of everything that can have an opposite.

For if a thing is opposite to another thing in its action, but not in its other states, then only their actions are of this description; if they are opposed in their quality, their qualities are of this description; and if they are opposed in their substance, their substances are of this description.

Now if the First had an opposite, He would stand to His opposite in this way. It would follow that it is the nature of each of them to perish, and that it is possible for the First to be annulled by His opposite, and this in His substance. But what can perish does not have its subsistence and permanence in its substance; rather its substance would not be sufficient for it to remain existent, nor would its substance be sufficient for it to come to be existent; this would be through something else. And what can fail to exist cannot be eternal; and that whose substance is not sufficient for its permanence or its existence has another cause, other than itself, for its existence or its permanence, and so it would not be first. Further, its existence would be only through the non-existence of its opposite; the non-existence of its opposite would then be the cause of its existence, and so it would not be the First Cause absolutely.

Further, the two would necessarily have some common place that receives them both, so that by meeting in it each could annul the other: either a substrate, or a genus, or something else besides these. That would be fixed, and these two would succeed one another upon it. That, then, would be prior in existence to each of them.

And if someone posits as the opposite of a thing something that is not of this description, what he posits is not an opposite, but something distinct with a kind of distinctness other than the distinctness of an opposite.

We do not deny that the First may have other things distinct from Him, with a distinctness other than that of an opposite, and other than that of something that would have His existence. Hence there cannot be any existent at the rank of His existence, for two opposites are at one rank of existence. The First is therefore alone in His existence; nothing else whatever that exists shares with Him in the species of His existence. He is therefore one, and He is, besides, alone in His rank. In this respect too, then, He is one.
IV. On the Denial of a Definition to Him, Glory Be to Him

Further, He is not divisible in account into things by which He is constituted as a substance. For the account that explains what He is cannot signify any one of His parts, or its two parts, by which He would be constituted. If it were so, the parts by which He is constituted would be causes of His existence, in the way that the notions signified by the parts of a thing's definition are causes of the existence of the thing defined, and in the way that matter and form are causes of the existence of what is composed of them. That is not possible in Him, since He is first and there is no cause of His existence at all.

Since He is not divisible in these ways, He is still further from being divisible into the divisions of quantity and the other kinds of division. From this it follows necessarily, too, that He has no magnitude and is not a body at all. In this respect too He is one.

For one of the meanings in which “one” is said is what is not divided; everything that is not divided in some respect is one in that respect in which it is not divided. If this is in respect of its action, it is one in that respect; if in respect of its quality, it is one in respect of quality; and what is not divided in its substance is one in its substance. Hence the First is undivided in His substance.
Va. On the Fact that His Oneness Is His Very Essence, and that He, Exalted, Is Knowing and Wise, and that He Is True, Living, and Life

The existence by which He is set apart from the other existents cannot be other than that by which He exists in His essence. Therefore His being set apart from everything other than Him is His being one in His essence.

For one of the meanings of unity is the proper existence by which each existent is set apart from everything else; it is by this that each existent is called one, in so far as it exists with the existence proper to it. And this meaning among the meanings of “one” is convertible with “existent”. In this way too, then, the First is one, and more entitled than any other one to the name “one” and to its meaning.

Because He is not matter and has no matter in any way, He is by His substance intellect in act. For what prevents a form from being intellect and from intellecting in act is the matter in which the thing exists; when a thing does not need matter for its existence, that thing is by its substance intellect in act. That is the state of the First; He is therefore intellect in act. He is also intelligible by His substance, for what prevents a thing from being intelligible in act is likewise matter. And He is intelligible in so far as He is intellect; for that whose identity is intellect does not need, in order to be intelligible, another essence outside it to intellect it. Rather it intellects its own essence by itself, and so, by intellecting its essence, it becomes intellecting and intellect in act, and, by its essence intellecting it, intelligible in act.

Likewise, in order to be intellect in act and intellecting in act, He does not need an essence that He would intellect and acquire from outside; rather He is intellect and intellecting by intellecting His own essence. For the essence that intellects is the one that is intellected, and so He is intellect in so far as He is intelligible. That He is intellect, that He is intelligible, and that He is intellecting are all one essence and one undivided substance.

A human being, for example, is intelligible, but what is intelligible of him is not intelligible in act; rather it was intelligible in potentiality and then became intelligible in act after the intellect had intellected it. So what is intelligible of a human being is not what intellects, nor is the intellect in him ever what is intelligible; nor is our own intellect, in so far as it is intellect, intelligible. We are intellecting, but not because our substance is intellect; for what we intellect is not that by which we are constituted as substance. The First is not like this; rather intellect, intellecting and intelligible are in Him one meaning, one essence, and one undivided substance.
Vb. He Is Knowing

So too with His being knowing. He does not need, in order to know, another essence outside His own essence, by knowing which He would acquire excellence; nor, in order to be known, another essence that knows Him. Rather He is sufficient by His substance both to know and to be known. His knowledge of His essence is nothing other than His substance; that He knows, that He is known, and that He is knowledge are one essence and one substance.
Vc. He Is Wise

So too with His being wise. For wisdom is to intellect the most excellent things by the most excellent knowledge; and by intellecting His own essence and knowing it, He knows the most excellent of things. The most excellent knowledge is the permanent knowledge that cannot cease, and that is His knowledge of His essence.
Vd. He Is True

So too with His being true. For the true is convertible with existence, and reality too is convertible with existence; for the reality of a thing is the existence proper to it, and the most perfect existence that is its share of existence.

Further, “true” is said of the intelligible by which the intellect comes upon the existent so as to correspond to it. That existent, in so far as it is intelligible, is called true; and in respect of its own essence, without being related to what intellects it, it is called existent.

The First is called true in both ways together: in that the existence that is His is the most perfect existence, and in that He is an intelligible by which whoever intellects Him comes upon the existent as it exists.

He does not need, in order to be true in so far as He is intelligible, another essence outside Him to intellect Him. He is also the most entitled to be called true in both ways together; and His reality is nothing other than His being true.
Ve. He Is Living and Life

So too with His being living and His being life: these two do not signify two essences but one essence. For the meaning of “living” is that it intellects the most excellent intelligible by the most excellent intellect, or knows the most excellent object of knowledge by the most excellent knowledge. Thus we are first called living when we perceive the lowest of perceptible things by the lowest perception; for we are called living when we perceive the sensibles, which are the lowest of the objects of knowledge, by sensation, which is the lowest of perceptions, and by the lowest of the perceiving faculties, which are the senses .

Therefore that which is the most excellent intellect, when it intellects and knows the most excellent intelligibles by the most excellent knowledge, is more fitting to be living; for it intellects in so far as it is intellect. That He is intellecting, that He is intellect, that He is knowing, and that He is knowledge are in Him one meaning; and likewise that He is living and that He is life are one meaning.

Further, the name “living” is sometimes transferred to what is not an animal. It is said of every existent that has reached its final perfection, and of everything that has attained such a degree of existence and perfection that there proceeds from it what it is its nature to produce, in the way that it is its nature to produce it. In this sense, since the First's existence is the most perfect existence, He is more entitled to the name “living” than anything to which the name is applied by transference.

Whatever is more complete in existence, when it is known and intellected, what is intellected and known of it is more complete; for the intelligible of it in our souls corresponds to what exists of it. In accordance with its existence outside our souls, its intelligible in our souls corresponds to its existence; and if it is deficient in existence, its intelligible in our souls is a more deficient intelligible.

Motion, time, the infinite, non-existence and existents like them: the intelligible of each of them in our souls is a deficient intelligible, since they are in themselves existents deficient in existence. Number, the triangle, the square and the like: their intelligibles in our souls are more perfect, because they are in themselves more perfect in existence. Therefore, in the case of the First, since He is at the utmost perfection of existence, the intelligible of Him in our souls ought likewise to be at the limit of perfection. Yet we find the matter otherwise. We must know, then, that on His side He is not hard to apprehend, since He is at the limit of perfection; but because of the weakness of the faculties of our intellects, and their entanglement with matter and non-existence, He is hard to apprehend, it is difficult for us to conceive Him, and we are too weak to intellect Him as His existence is. For the excess of His perfection dazzles us, so that we lack the strength to conceive Him completely.

So it is with light. Light is the first of visible things, the most perfect and the most manifest of them; by it all other visible things become visible, and it is the cause of colours becoming visible. One would expect that the more complete and the greater it is, the more complete sight's perception of it would be. Yet we see the matter to be the opposite: the greater it is, the weaker our seeing of it. This is not because it is hidden or deficient; in itself it is at the utmost of manifestness and luminosity. But its perfection, in so far as it is light, dazzles the eyes, so that the eyes are bewildered by it.

Such is the case of the First Cause, the First Intellect and the First Truth with respect to our own intellects. The deficiency of the intelligible of Him with us is not due to any deficiency in Himself, nor is our difficulty in apprehending Him due to any difficulty in His existence; rather it is because of the weakness of the faculties of our intellects that conceiving Him is difficult. So the intelligibles that are in our souls are deficient, and our conception of them is weak.

This is of two kinds. One kind cannot, on account of its own essence, be conceived and intellected with a complete conception, because of the weakness of its existence and the deficiency of its essence and substance. The other kind is, on its own side, freely open to being understood and conceived completely and in the most perfect way possible; but our minds and the faculties of our intellects are prevented, by their weakness and their distance from the substance of that thing, from conceiving it completely and as it is in the perfection of its existence.
Each of these two kinds stands at the far extreme of existence from the other: one at the limit of perfection, the other at the limit of deficiency.

Since we are bound up with matter, and matter is the cause of our substances having become a substance remote from the First Substance, it follows that the nearer our substances come to it, the more complete, the more certain and the truer our conception of it. That is, the nearer we are to separation from matter, the more complete our conception of Him; and we become nearer to Him only by our substance becoming intellect in act. When we have separated from matter completely, the intelligible of Him in our minds becomes as perfect as it can be.
VI. On His Greatness, Majesty and Glory, Exalted Be He

So too with His greatness, majesty and glory. Greatness, majesty and glory in a thing exist only according to its perfection, whether in its substance or in an accident among its properties. Most often they are said of us only on account of the perfection of something we have in one of our accidents, such as wealth and knowledge, or in some accident of the body.
And since the First's perfection surpasses every perfection, His greatness, majesty and glory surpass everything that possesses greatness and glory.

His greatness and glory are the utmost limits in what He has from His substance, not in anything else outside His substance and essence. He is great in His essence and glorious in His essence, whether or not another exalts Him, whether or not another magnifies Him, whether or not another glorifies Him.

Beauty, splendour and adornment in every existent consist in its existing with its most excellent existence and attaining its final perfection. Since the First's existence is the most excellent existence, His beauty exceeds the beauty of everything that has beauty, and so too His adornment and His splendour. Moreover, all of these are His in His substance and essence; and that is in Himself and through His intellecting His own essence. As for us, our beauty, adornment and splendour belong to us through our accidents, not through our essence, and through things outside us, not in our substance. But beauty and perfection in Him are nothing other than one essence; and so with the rest of these.

Pleasure, joy and delight arise and are produced chiefly by perceiving the most beautiful, the most splendid and the most adorned with the most exact and complete perception. Since He is the most beautiful without limit, the most splendid and the most adorned, His perception of His own essence is the most exact perception to the utmost degree, and His knowledge of His substance is the most excellent knowledge absolutely.

The pleasure that the First takes is a pleasure whose essence we do not understand and the measure of whose greatness we do not know, except by comparison and by relation to the pleasure we find when we have perceived what is, for us, most perfect and most splendid, with the most exact and complete perception, whether by sensation, by imagination, or by intellectual knowledge. In that state there comes to us a pleasure that we suppose surpasses every pleasure in greatness, and we count ourselves blessed to the utmost with what we have attained of it, even though that state of ours is short-lived and quickly passes.

The relation of His knowledge and perception of the most excellent, the most beautiful and the most splendid, which is His own essence, to our knowledge and perception of what is for us most beautiful and most splendid, is the relation of His joy, pleasure and delight in Himself to the pleasure, joy and delight we attain in ourselves.

And since there is no relation between our perception and His perception, nor between what we know and what He knows, nor between what is most beautiful for us and the most beautiful of His essence, or, if there is a relation, it is a slight one, there is therefore no relation between our pleasure, joy and delight in ourselves and what the First has of these; or, if there is a relation, it is a very slight one. For how can there be a relation between what is a small part and what is infinite in measure in time, or between what is very deficient and what is at the utmost of perfection?

And since whatever takes more pleasure in its essence, rejoices in it more, and delights in it with a greater delight, loves its essence, loves it passionately and admires it more, it is evident that the First passionately loves His essence, loves it and admires it, in proportion. The relation of this to our passionate love for the excellence of our essence, in which we take pleasure, is as the relation of the excellence of His own essence and the perfection of His essence to our own excellence and perfection, which we admire in ourselves.
Love in Him is itself the beloved; what admires in Him is what is admired; the passionate lover in Him is the passionately loved.

This is the contrary of what is found in us. For what we passionately love is excellence and beauty, but what passionately loves in us is not beauty and excellence; the lover has another faculty, which does not belong to the passionately loved, and so the lover in us is not itself the passionately loved. With Him, however, the passionate lover in Him is itself the passionately loved, and love is the beloved. He is therefore the first beloved and the first object of passionate love, whether or not another loves Him, and whether or not another passionately loves Him.

parts.name: VII. On How All Existents Proceed from Him

lines.text: VII. On How All Existents Proceed from Him

The First is that from which whatever exists has come to exist. Once the First has the existence that is His, it follows necessarily that from Him there exist all the other existents whose existence is not by human will and choice, with the kind of existence they have, part of which is witnessed by the senses and part known by demonstration.

The existence of what exists from Him is only by way of an emanation of His existence for the existence of something else, and in such a way that the existence of what is other than Him emanates from His own existence. In this way the existence of what exists from Him is not in any respect a cause of Him, nor is it an end for the existence of the First, as the existence of a son, in so far as he is a son, is an end for the existence of the parents in so far as they are parents. That is, the existence that comes from Him does confer any perfection on Him, as happens to us with most of the things that come from us: for example, by giving money to others we acquire from them honour or pleasure or some other good, so that these produce some perfection in the giver.

The First's existence is not for the sake of anything else, nor do other things exist through Him in such a way that the purpose of His existence would be that all other things should exist; for then His existence would have a cause outside Him, and He would not be first. Nor, by giving existence to what is other than Him, does He attain a perfection He did not have before, beyond the perfection in which He is, as one who is generous with his wealth or with something else attains, by what he spends, pleasure or honour or rule or some other good.
All these things are impossible in the First, for they would do away with His being first and His priority, and would make something else prior to Him and a cause of His existence.
Rather, His existence is for the sake of His own essence; and it attaches to His substance and His existence, and follows from it, that something other than Him should exist from Him.

Therefore His existence, through which existence emanates to another, is in His substance; and His existence, through which He is constituted as substance in His essence, is the very same existence through which the existence of another comes about from Him.

He is not divided into two things, by one of which His essence would be constituted as substance and by the other of which something else would come about from Him, in the way that we have two things: by one of them, rationality, we are constituted as substance, and by the other, the art of writing, we write. Rather He is one essence and one substance, by which He is constituted as substance, and by that very same thing something else comes about from Him.

Nor does He need, in order that the existence of something else should emanate from His existence, anything other than His essence that would be in Him, nor an accident in Him, nor a motion by which He would acquire a state He did not have, nor an instrument outside His essence: as fire, in order that vapour should come from it and from water, needs heat by which the water is turned into vapour; or as the sun, in order to heat what is around us, needs to move, so that by motion it acquires a state it did not have, and then from it, and through the state it acquired by motion, heat arises in what is around us.
Or as the carpenter needs the axe and the saw, so that separation, cutting and splitting may come about from him in the wood.

Nor is His existence, through which the existence of another emanates from Him, more perfect than His existence that is by His substance; nor is His existence that is by His substance more perfect than that from which the existence of another emanates. Rather the two together are one essence. Nor can there be any hindrance to Him, whether from Himself or from outside at all, that would prevent the existence of another from emanating from Him.
VIII. On the Ranks of the Existents

The existents are many, and for all their multitude they differ in rank. His substance is a substance from which every existence emanates, whatever that existence may be, perfect or deficient. His substance is also such that, when all the existents emanate from it in the order of their ranks, there comes from Him to each existent the share of existence that belongs to it, and its rank in existence.

It begins with the most perfect of them in existence; then follows what is slightly less perfect; and after that the less and less perfect continue to follow, until it ends at the existent such that, if one passed beyond it to what is below it, one would pass to what cannot exist at all; and there the existents cease from existence. And because His substance is a substance from which all the existents emanate, without its being restricted to one existence rather than another, He is generous, and His generosity lies in His substance. The existents are ordered from Him, and each existent receives its share of existence according to its rank from Him; so He is just, and His justice lies in His substance, and it is not due to anything outside His substance.

His substance is also such that, when the existents have come about ordered in their ranks, they are combined, linked and ordered with one another, in a combination, linkage and order through which the many things become a single whole and come to be as one thing. That through which they are linked and combined lies, for some things, in their substances, so that their substances, through which they exist, are the very things through which they are combined and linked. For other things it lies in states in them that follow upon their substances, such as love, through which human beings are linked to one another: it is a state in them, not their substances through which they exist. This too is acquired by them from the First, for it lies in the substance of the First that there should come from Him, in many of the existents, together with their substances, the states through which they are linked, combined and ordered with one another.
IX. On the Names by Which the First, Exalted Be His Glory, Should Be Called

The names by which the First should be called are the names that signify, in the existents we have, and then in the most excellent of them in our eyes, perfection and excellence of existence; but without any of those names signifying in Him the perfection and excellence that those names are customarily used to signify in the existents we have and in the most excellent of them. Rather, they signify the perfection that is proper to Him in His substance.

Further, the kinds of perfection that those many names are customarily used to signify are many. But one must not think that the kinds of His perfections signified by His many names are many kinds into which the First is divided and by all of which together He is made a substance. Rather, by those many names one should signify a single substance and a single existence, not divided at all.

Of the names that signify perfection and excellence in the things we have, some signify what belongs to the thing in itself, not insofar as it is related to something else outside it, such as "existent", "one" and "living"; and some signify what belongs to the thing by relation to something else outside it, such as "just" and "generous". In the things we have, these names signify an excellence and a perfection whose relation to something else outside it is a part of that perfection, so that the relation is a part of the whole of what those names signify, since that name, or that excellence and that perfection, is constituted by the relation to something else.

When names of this kind are transferred and the First is called by them, we intend to signify by them the relation He has to others through the existence that has emanated from Him. We must then not make the relation a part of His perfection, nor make the perfection signified by that name be constituted by that relation. Rather, we must signify by it a substance and a perfection upon which that relation necessarily follows; and signify that the relation is constituted by that substance, and that the relation follows from what is the substance of that substance which that name signifies.
X. On the Secondary Existents and How the Many Proceed

From the First there emanates the existence of the Second. This Second is likewise a substance not embodied at all, nor is it in matter. It intellects its own essence and intellects the First, and what it intellects of its own essence is nothing other than its essence. Through what it intellects of the First, the existence of a Third follows from it; and through its being made a substance by its own proper essence, the existence of the first heaven follows from it.

The Third, too, has its existence not in matter; by its substance it is an intellect, and it intellects its own essence and intellects the First. Through that by which it is made a substance in its own proper essence, the existence of the sphere of the fixed stars follows from it.

Through what it intellects of the First, the existence of a Fourth follows from it. This too is not in matter. It intellects its own essence and intellects the First. Through that by which it is made a substance in its own proper essence, the existence of the sphere of Saturn follows from it; and through what it intellects of the First, the existence of a Fifth follows from it. This Fifth, too, has its existence not in matter; it intellects its own essence and intellects the First. Through that by which it is made a substance in its essence, the existence of the sphere of Jupiter follows from it; and through what it intellects of the First, the existence of a Sixth follows from it. This too has its existence not in matter, and it intellects its own essence and intellects the First. Through that by which it is made a substance in its essence, the existence of the sphere of Mars follows from it; and through what it intellects of the First, the existence of a Seventh follows from it.

This too has its existence not in matter, and it intellects its own essence and intellects the First. Through that by which it is made a substance in its essence, the existence of the sphere of the Sun follows from it; and through what it intellects of the First, the existence of an Eighth follows from it. This too has its existence not in matter; it intellects its own essence and intellects the First. Through that by which it is made a substance in its own proper essence, the existence of the sphere of Venus follows from it; and through what it intellects of the First, the existence of a Ninth follows from it. This too has its existence not in matter; it intellects its own essence and intellects the First. Through that by which it is made a substance in its essence, the existence of the sphere of Mercury follows from it; and through what it intellects of the First, the existence of a Tenth follows from it.

This too has its existence not in matter, and it intellects its own essence and intellects the First. Through that by which it is made a substance in its essence, the existence of the sphere of the Moon follows from it; and through what it intellects of the First, the existence of an Eleventh follows from it. This Eleventh, too, has its existence not in matter, and it intellects its own essence and intellects the First. But with it there comes to an end the existence whose possessor needs no matter and no substrate at all.

These are the separate things, which in their substances are intellects and intelligibles. And with the sphere of the Moon there comes to an end the existence of the heavenly bodies, which are those that by their nature move in a circle.
XI. On the Existents and the Bodies That Are With Us

These existents that we have enumerated are those to which their most excellent perfections belonged in their substances from the very beginning; and with these two the existence of such things comes to an end. Those that come after these two are things whose nature it is not to exist in their most excellent perfections in their substances from the beginning. Rather, it is their nature to have first the most deficient of their modes of existence, and to begin from it and rise little by little until each species of them reaches its utmost perfection in its substance, and then in the rest of its accidents. This condition lies in the nature of this genus, without its being something introduced into it from anything else foreign to it. Of these, some are natural, some voluntary, and some composed of the natural and the voluntary. The natural among them is a preparation for the voluntary and precedes the voluntary in time, and the voluntary among them cannot exist unless the natural among them has existed before.

The natural bodies among these are the elements, such as fire, air, water and earth, and what is akin to them, such as vapour, flame and the like; the minerals, such as stones and their kinds; plants; the non-rational animal; and the rational animal.
XII. On Matter and Form

Each of these is constituted of two things. One of them stands as the wood of a bed stands, and the other as the shape of the bed. What stands as the wood is the matter, or hyle; what stands as its shape is the form and configuration; and so with whatever things are akin to these two. Matter is set as a substrate so that the form may subsist through it, and the form cannot have subsistence and existence without matter. So matter exists for the sake of the form; and if no form existed, there would be no matter.

The form does not exist in order that the matter may exist through it, but in order that the corporeal substance may come to be a substance in act. For every species comes to exist in act, and in its most perfect existence, only when its form has come about; and as long as its matter exists without its form, it is that species only in potency. The wood of a bed, as long as it is without the form of a bed, is a bed in potency, and it becomes a bed in act only when its form comes about in its matter. The more deficient of the thing's two existences is through its matter, and the more perfect of its two existences is through the form.
The forms of these bodies are contrary to one another, and each of them can exist and can fail to exist.

The matter of each of them is receptive of its form and of the contrary of that form: the form of the thing may exist in it, and may fail to exist in it; indeed the matter may exist under a form other than that one.

The elements are four, and their forms are contrary to one another. The matter of each of them is receptive of the form of that element and of its contrary. The matter of each of them is common to all of them, and it is the matter both of them and of all the other bodies beneath the heavenly bodies, since everything beneath the heavenly bodies comes to be from the elements. The matters of the elements have no matters of their own; so they are the first matters, common to everything beneath the heavenly bodies. None of these is given its form from the beginning. Rather, each of the bodies is first given only its matter, through which it exists in remote potency only, not in act, since what was given to it was only its first matter. For this reason it is always striving toward the form by which it is made a substance, and it does not cease rising little by little until it attains its form, by which it exists in act.
XIII. On the Apportioning of Ranks Between the Material Bodies and the Divine Existents
The order of these existents is that the lowest of them is put first, then the more and more excellent, until it ends at the most excellent of them, than which there is nothing more excellent.

The lowest of them is the common first matter; more excellent than it are the elements; then the minerals; then plants; then the non-rational animal; then the rational animal. And after the rational animal there is nothing more excellent than it.

As for the existents mentioned earlier, they are ordered with the most excellent of them first, then the more and more deficient, until it ends at the most deficient of them. The most excellent and most perfect of them is the First.

Of the things that come from the First, the most excellent on the whole are those that are neither bodies nor in bodies; after them come the heavenly ones. The most excellent of the separate ones among these is the Second, then the rest of them in order, until it ends at the Eleventh.
The most excellent of the heavenly ones is the first heaven, then the second, then the rest of them in order, until it ends at the eleventh, which is the sphere of the Moon.
The separate things after the First are ten, and the heavenly bodies in all are nine; so all of them together are nineteen.

Each one of the ten is unique in its existence and its rank, and its existence cannot belong to anything other than it. For if another shared its existence with it, that other, if it is other than this one, must necessarily have something by which it differs from this one; and that by which it differs from this one would be its own proper existence; so the existence proper to that thing would not be that by which this one exists. Hence their existence would not be one existence; rather each of the two would have something proper to it.
Nor can it have a contrary; for whatever has a contrary has a matter shared between it and its contrary, and none of these can have matter.

Further, what falls under a species has many individuals only because the substrates of the form of that species are many. So for what has no matter, there cannot be anything else in its species besides it.

Further, contraries arise only either from things whose substances are contrary, or from one thing whose states and relations in its substrate are contrary. Such are cold and heat: both come from the sun, but the sun is in two different states, of nearness and remoteness, and through its two states it produces contrary states and relations.

The First cannot have a contrary; nor are His states contrary with respect to the Second, nor is His relation to the Second a contrary relation. Nor can there be contrariety in the Second, nor likewise in the Third, and so on until one reaches the Tenth.

Each one of the ten intellects its own essence and intellects the First. None of them is sufficient to be excellent in existence by intellecting its own essence alone; rather, it gains complete excellence by intellecting, together with its own essence, the essence of the First Cause. And in proportion as the excellence of the First exceeds the excellence of its own essence, its joy in itself through what it intellects of the First is greater than its joy in itself when it intellects its own essence. Likewise its pleasure in itself through what it intellects of the First exceeds its pleasure through what it intellects of its own essence, in proportion as the perfection of the First exceeds the perfection of its own essence; and its admiration of itself, and its passionate love for itself, through what it intellects of the First, exceed its admiration of itself and its passionate love for itself through what it intellects of its own essence, in proportion as the splendour and beauty of the First exceed the splendour and beauty of its own essence. So it is, in its own eyes, loved first and admired first through what it intellects of the First, and secondly through what it intellects of its own essence. The First, then, in relation to these ten, is also the first beloved and the first object of passionate love.
XIV. On What the Heavenly Bodies Have in Common

The heavenly bodies are nine wholes in nine ranks, each whole contained by a single spherical body. The first of them contains one body only, and so it moves with a single circular motion, very swift. The second is one body containing bodies whose motion is shared: they have two motions only, and all of them share in both motions together. The third and those after it, completing the seven, each contain many bodies, which differ in the motions proper to each of them and share in other motions. The genus of all these bodies is one, but they differ in species; and in each species there can exist only one in number, which nothing else shares in that species. For nothing else of its species shares with the Sun in its existence: it is unique in its existence; and so too the Moon and the rest of the stars.

These are akin to the material existents, in that they have substrates resembling the matters that underlie forms, and things in them that are like forms; and those things subsist in those substrates. Their forms, however, cannot have contraries; the substrate of each of them cannot be receptive of any form other than that one, nor can it be empty of it. And because there is no privation in any way at all in the substrates of their forms, and their forms have no privations opposed to them, their substrates do not prevent their forms from intellecting and from being intellects in their own essence.
So each of these is, by its form, an intellect in act; by it, it intellects the essence of the separate one from which the existence of that body comes, and it intellects the First.

Yet not all that it intellects of its own essence is intellect, for it intellects its substrate, and its substrate does not intellect. And since it does not intellect by its substrate, but only by its form, there is in it an intelligible that does not intellect. So it intellects everything by which it is made a substance and given form; that is to say, its being a substance is by a form and a substrate. By this it differs from the First and from the ten, which are free of matter and of every substrate.

Man shares matter with it. It too rejoices in its essence, not only through what it intellects of its own essence, but through what it intellects of the First, and then through what it intellects of the essence of the separate one from which its existence comes. And it shares with the separate one in its passionate love for the First, and in its admiration of itself for the splendour and beauty it has gained from the First; but in all of this it falls far short of the ten.

Of everything that the material things share with it, it has the noblest and most excellent. Thus of shapes it has the most excellent, the spherical; of the visible qualities, the most excellent, which is light: for some of its parts produce light, namely the stars, and some of its parts are transparent in act, since they are filled with light from themselves and from what they receive from the stars; and of motions it has the most excellent, circular motion. It shares with the ten in having been given, from its very beginning, the most excellent of that by which it is made a substance; and so too its magnitudes, its shapes, and the visible quality proper to it.

parts.name: XV. On That in Which and Toward Which the Heavenly Bodies Move, and For What They Move

lines.text: XV. On That in Which and Toward Which the Heavenly Bodies Move, and For What They Move

It differs from the ten in that the heavenly bodies could not be given, from their very beginning, that toward which they move; and that toward which they move is among the slightest and lowest of the accidents that occur in a body.

That is because every body is in some "where", and the kind of "where" that belongs to this body is to be around some body: its "where" is of this kind. So it is not possible for it, as a whole, to move out of the whole of this kind.

But this kind has parts, and the body that is in it has parts; and no part of this body has a better claim than another to any one part of what lies around. Rather, every part of the body must have every part of what lies around, and must not have a better claim to it at one time than at another, but at every time, always. Whenever a part of this body comes to be at some part of what lies around, it needs also to have the part that lies before it. And it cannot have both parts together at one time.

So it must leave the part where it is and pass to the one before it, until it has gone through every part of what lies around. And because the part where it was has no better claim to it at one time than at another, it must have that part always; and since that part cannot be its always while remaining one in number, it becomes one in species, by being its at one time and not at another.

Then it returns to one like it in species, then leaves that too for a time, then returns to a third like it, and leaves that too for a time, then returns to a fourth like it; and so it is with it forever.

It is evident, then, that the positions from which it moves, through which it passes, and to which it returns, are in its relation to the body around which the heaven lies. The meaning of "relation" is that one says "this is toward this", "this is from this", and the like; for the meaning of "where" is the relation of a body to the surface of the body that fits around it.

Every heavenly body is in a sphere, that is, a solid circle; and the relations of its parts to the parts of the surface of the bodies beneath it change constantly, and each of them returns in time to come to relations like those that went before.
The relation of one thing to another is the lowest thing that it has, and the most remote of accidents from the substance of the thing.

Each of the spheres and solid circles that has a motion of its own is either swifter or slower in motion than another, such as the sphere of Saturn and the sphere of the Moon; for the sphere of the Moon is swifter in motion than the sphere of Saturn.
XVI. On the States in Which the Circular Motions Exist, and on the Nature They Share

This difference of degree in their motions is not according to their relation to anything else; it belongs to them in themselves and essentially. The slow among them is always slow, and the swift always swift.

Further, many of the heavenly bodies differ in their positions relative to the centre and to what is beneath them; and because of this difference in their positions, there attaches to each of them a property, accidentally, that it moves swiftly around the earth at times and slowly at times.

This is apart from the constant swiftness of some and the constant slowness of others, as with the motion of Saturn compared with the motion of the Moon. There also attaches to them, by the relation of some to others, that they come together at times and separate at times, and that some stand to others in contrary relations. Further, they come near at times to some of what is beneath them, and move away from it at times; they are visible at times and hidden at times. These contraries attach to them not in their substances, nor in the accidents close to their substances, but in their relations.
Such are rising and setting: they are two contrary relations of theirs to what is beneath them.

The heavenly body is the first of the existents to which contrary things attach; and the first things in which there is contrariety are the relations of this body to what is beneath it, and the relations of these bodies to one another. These contraries are the lowest of contraries, and contrariety is a deficiency in existence. So deficiency attaches to the heavenly body in the lowest of the things that are apt to exist.

All the heavenly bodies also have a common nature, and it is through it that they all move with the motion of the first body among them, a circular motion in a day and a night. For this motion does not belong to what is beneath the first heaven by compulsion, since there can be nothing in the heaven that runs its course by compulsion. Among them there is also a difference in their substances, without contrariety, such as the difference of Saturn from Jupiter, of every star from every other star, and of every sphere from every other sphere. Then, as we have said, contrariety attaches to them in their relations, and those relations and their contraries change and succeed one another upon them.

So they leave one relation and pass to its contrary, then return to the one they had left, in species, not in number. Thus they have relations that recur, some returning in a longer period and some in a shorter, and states and relations that do not recur at all. And it attaches to them that a group of them have contrary relations to one single thing, as when some of them are near a thing and some far from that very same thing.
XVII. On the Causes From Which the First Form and the First Matter Arise

From the common nature that they have there follows the existence of the first matter, common to everything beneath them; from the difference of their substances, the existence of many bodies differing in substance; from the contrariety of their relations and correlations, the existence of the contrary forms; and from the change of contrary relations upon them and their succession, the change of contrary forms upon the first matter and their succession.

From the occurrence of contrary relations and conflicting correlations to one single essence at one time, on the part of a group of bodies, there follows a mingling among the things that have contrary forms, and their mixtures; and from the kinds of those different mixtures there arise many species of bodies. From their correlations that recur and return there arise the things whose existence recurs and returns, some in a shorter period and some in a longer. And from those of their correlations and states that do not recur, but arise only at some one time, without having been before and without arising afterward, there arise the things that come to be and do not recur at all.
XVIII. On the Ranks of the Material Bodies in Coming to Be

First the elements come to be; then the bodies akin to them and associated with them, such as vapours and their kinds, for example clouds and winds and everything else that occurs in the air; and likewise what is akin to them around the earth and beneath it, and in water and fire.

And there arise in the elements, and in each of the rest of these, powers by which they move of themselves toward things that are apt to belong to them, or to exist through them, without a mover from outside; powers by which some act on others; and powers by which some receive the action of others. Then the heavenly bodies act on them, and they act on one another; and from the combination of actions from these directions there arise many kinds of minglings and mixtures, and many proportions, differing without contrariety and differing by contrariety.

From these there follows the existence of all the other bodies. First the elements mix with one another, and from this there arise many contrary bodies. Then these contraries mix, some only with one another, and some with one another and with the elements; that is a second mixing after the first, and from it there arise, again, many bodies with contrary forms.

In each of these, too, there arise powers by which some act on others, powers by which they receive the action of another upon them, and powers by which they move of themselves without a mover from outside. Then the heavenly bodies act on them as well, and they act on one another; the elements act on them, and they in turn act on the elements.

From the combination of these actions in different ways there arise many further mixings, by which they move far away from the elements and from the first matter. They continue to mix, one mixing after another that preceded it, the second mixing always being more composite than the one before, until bodies arise that cannot mix in such a way that another body, further from the elements than they, would arise from their mixing; and so the mixing stops.
So some bodies arise from the first mixing, some from the second, some from the third, and some from the last mixing.

The minerals arise from a mixing nearer to the elements and less composite, and their distance from the elements is by fewer ranks. Plants arise from a mixing more composite than theirs and further from the elements by more ranks. The non-rational animal arises from a mixing more composite than that of plants. And man alone is the one who arises from the last mixing.

In each of these species there arise powers by which it moves of itself, powers by which it acts on another, and powers by which it receives the action of another upon it. As for what among them acts on another, the subjects of its action are, in sum, three: those on which it acts more, those on which it acts less, and those on which it acts equally. Likewise what receives the action of another may be a subject for three kinds of agents: for what acts on it more, for what acts on it less, and for what acts on it equally.
The action of each one on each one is either by assisting it or by opposing it.

Then the heavenly bodies act on each of them, along with the action of some of them on others, by assisting some and opposing others. What they assist, they assist at one time and oppose at another; and what they oppose, they oppose at one time and assist at another. So the kinds of heavenly actions are joined in them with the actions of some of them on others, and from their conjunction there arise very many further mixtures and minglings, and in each species there arise very many, very different individuals.
These, then, are the causes of the existence of the natural things that are beneath the heavenly ones.
XIX. On the Succession of Forms upon Matter

In these ways their existence comes about in the first place. Once they exist, it would be their course to remain and endure. But since whatever is of this condition among the existents has its subsistence from matter and form, and the forms are contrary to one another, and every matter is such that both this form and its contrary can exist for it, each of these bodies came to have a right and a claim by virtue of its form, and a right and a claim by virtue of its matter. What is due to it by right of its form is that it remain in the existence it has; what is due to it by right of its matter is that it receive another existence, contrary to the existence it has. And since it is not possible to give both of these their due together at one time, it follows necessarily that the one is given its due at one time, so that the thing exists and remains for some period with its existence preserved, then perishes and its contrary comes into existence, and that in turn remains; and so on forever. For the existence of neither of them has a better claim than the existence of the other, nor the persistence of either a better claim than the persistence of the other, since each of them has a share of existence and persistence.

Further, since one and the same matter is shared between two contraries, and the subsistence of each of the two contraries is through it, and the matter has no better claim to one of the two contraries than to the other, and it cannot be given to both of them at one time, it follows necessarily that this matter is given this contrary at some times and that contrary at other times, and that they alternate upon it.

So each of the two comes to be as if it had a right held by the other: with each there is something that belongs to the other, and with the other something that belongs to it. Each of them, then, holds a right that ought to pass to each from each. Justice in this is that the matter of this one be found and given to that one, or the matter of that one be found and given to this one, and that this alternate between them. Because of the need to fulfil justice in these existents, it was not possible for a single thing to remain forever as one in number; so its persistence through all time was made to be as one in species. And for a thing to remain one in species, the individuals of that species must exist for some period and then perish, and other individuals of that species take their place; and so it goes, always after this pattern.

Of these, some are elements, and some come to be from their mixture. Of those that come from their mixture, some come from a mixture of greater composition and some from a mixture of lesser composition. As for the elements, the destroying contrary of each of them is from outside only, since it has no contrary within the whole of its body. As for what comes to be from a mixture of little composition, the contraries in it are few and their powers broken and weak; for that reason the destroying contrary within it is weak in power and destroys it only by means of something from outside, so that its destroying contrary is likewise from outside. What comes from a mixture of lesser composition, then, has its destroying contraries from outside only. But in those that come from a mixture of greater composition, through the multitude of the contraries in them and of their compositions, the contrariety among the mixed things is more manifest, the powers of the contraries in them are strong, and they act upon one another together; for since they are made of dissimilar parts, nothing prevents there being contrariety in them, so that the contrary that destroys such a thing is from outside its body and from inside it together.

Those bodies that are destroyed by their contrary from outside do not continually dissolve of themselves, such as stones and sand; for these two and what is of their kind dissolve only from external things. But the others, plants and animals, dissolve also from things contrary to them within. Therefore, if any of these is long-lived, its form remains for some period through something constantly replacing what dissolves from its body. That thing only takes the place of what dissolves; and nothing can replace what dissolves from its body and join itself to that body unless it strips off the form it had and puts on the form of this very body. That is, the body is nourished; and so a nutritive faculty was placed in these bodies, together with everything that assists this faculty, so that each of these bodies draws to itself something contrary to it, whose contrariety is then stripped from it; it receives it into itself and clothes it with the form in which it is itself wrapped, until over a long period this faculty gives out, and there dissolves from that body something the restoring power cannot replace with its like, and that body perishes with it. In this way it was protected against what dissolves it from within. Against what destroys it from outside, it was protected by the instruments given to it, some within it and some outside its body. So for the continuance of what continues as one in species, it needs other individuals to take the place of whatever of it perishes, standing in the place of those that have perished.

This comes about in one of two ways. Either, alongside the first individuals, there are other individuals that have been brought into existence from them, so that when those first ones perish these stand in their place, and at no time is there lacking the existence of some individual of that species, whether in that place or in another. Or what succeeds the first comes to be some time after the first has perished, so that a period passes in which no individual of that species exists. So in some of them powers were placed through which their like in species comes to be, and in others they were not placed.

In those in which it was not placed, the causes that bring into being a replacement for whatever of them perishes are the heavenly bodies alone, since these assist the elements in this. In that in which a power was placed through which its like in species comes to be, this happens through that power which it has, and joined to it is the action of the heavenly bodies and of the other bodies: either they give it aid, or they oppose it with an opposition that does not cancel the action of the power but produces a mixture, either one by which the action that comes from that power is brought into balance, or one that moves it a little or a great deal away from balance, to an extent that does not cancel its action. Then there comes to be what takes the place of what has perished of that species. All these things happen either for the most part, or for the lesser part, or equally. In this way the persistence of this genus of existents endures.

Each of these bodies has a right and a claim by virtue of its form, and a right and a claim by virtue of its matter. What is due to it by right of its form is that it remain in the existence it has and not pass away; what is due to it by right of its matter is that it receive another existence, opposite and contrary to the existence it has. Justice is that each of the two be given its full claim; and since it is not possible to give it this at one time, it follows necessarily that this one be given its due at one time and that one at another, so that the thing exists and remains for some period with its existence preserved, then perishes and its contrary comes to be; and so forever.

What preserves its existence is either a power in the body in which its form is; or a power in another body which is an instrument joined to it, serving it in the preservation of its existence; or the one charged with its preservation is some other body that rules over the thing preserved, namely the heavenly body or some other body; or this comes about through all of these together.

Further, since these existents are contrary to one another, the matter of every two contraries among them is shared. The matter that belongs to this body is itself also the matter of that one, and that which belongs to that one is itself also this one's. So with each of them there is something that belongs to the other, and with the other something that belongs to it; and it is as if each, in this respect, had with each a right that ought to pass to each from each. The matter that a thing has with another is either a matter whose course is to put on that thing's very form, like a body that is nourished by another body, or a matter whose course is to put on the form of its species, not its very form, like people who succeed people who have passed away.

Justice in this is that what this one holds of the matter of that one be found and given to that one, and what that one holds of the matter of this one be given by that one to this one. That by which a thing obtains its matter in full from its contrary and wrests it from it is either a power in it joined to its form in one body, and then that body is an inseparable instrument for it in this; or it is in another body, and then that is a separate instrument for it, serving it only in wresting matter from its contrary, while another power, in that body or in another, clothes it either with its very form or with the form of its species. Or it is a single power that does both things together. Or what obtains its right for it is another body in its own right, whether heavenly or otherwise. Or this comes about through all of these together.

A body becomes matter for another body only either by the other giving it its own form completely, or by the other clothing it with something of its own form and lessening its dignity. And a body that becomes an instrument for another, serving another body, likewise becomes an instrument only in one of these two ways: either by its form entirely, or by the other clothing it with a little of the dignity of its own form, to an extent that does not take it out of its quiddity, as one breaks the strength of slaves and subdues them until they are humbled and serve.
XX. On the Parts of the Human Soul and Its Faculties

When the human being comes to be, the first thing to arise in him is the faculty by which he is nourished, which is the nutritive faculty. After that comes the faculty by which he senses what is tangible, such as heat and cold, and the others: those by which he senses tastes, smells, sounds, and colours and all visible things, such as rays of light. Along with the senses there arises in him, through them, an appetition toward what he senses, so that he desires it or dislikes it. Then after that another faculty arises in him, by which he retains the impressions of sensibles in his soul after they have gone from the observation of the senses. This is the imaginative faculty. It combines sensibles with one another and separates them from one another in various combinations and separations, some false and some true; and joined to it is an appetition toward what it imagines.

Then after that the rational faculty arises in him, by which it is possible for him to intellect the intelligibles, by which he distinguishes between the noble and the base, and by which he acquires the arts and the sciences. Joined to it also is an appetition toward what he intellects.

Of the nutritive faculty there is one ruling faculty, and there are faculties that are its subsidiaries and servants. The ruling nutritive faculty is, among the organs of the body, in the mouth. The subsidiaries and servants are dispersed in the other organs, and each subsidiary and serving faculty is in some one of the other organs of the body.
The ruling one among them is by nature the governor of the other faculties; the other faculties imitate it and model their actions on what is by nature the aim of their ruler, which is in the heart.

This is like the stomach, the liver and the spleen, the organs that serve these, the organs that serve these servants, and those that serve these in turn. The liver is an organ that both rules and is ruled: it is ruled by the heart, and it rules the gall bladder, the kidney and organs like them. The bladder serves the kidney, the kidney serves the liver, and the liver serves the heart; and all the other organs are found to be after this manner.

The sensory faculty has a ruler and subsidiaries. Its subsidiaries are these five senses known to all, dispersed in the two eyes, the two ears and the rest. Each of these five perceives a sensation peculiar to it. The ruling one among them is the one in which everything that all five perceive is gathered. It is as if these five were heralds of that one, and as if they were bearers of reports, each charged with one kind of report and with the reports of one region of the realm; and the ruling one is like the king, with whom the reports of the regions of his realm are gathered from his reporters. The ruling one of these, too, is in the heart.

The imaginative faculty has no subsidiaries dispersed in other organs; rather it is one, and it too is in the heart. It retains the sensibles after they have gone from sense, and it is by nature a judge over the sensibles and has command over them: it separates some of them from others and combines some with others in various combinations, some of which happen to agree with what was sensed and some to differ from the sensed.

As for the rational faculty, it has no subsidiaries and no servants of its own kind in the other organs; rather its rule is over the other faculties, the imaginative among them. It is the ruler over the ruling member of every genus in which there is a ruler and a ruled: it is the ruler of the imaginative faculty, the ruler of the ruling sensory faculty, and the ruler of the ruling nutritive faculty.

The appetitive faculty, which is the one that longs for a thing or dislikes it, is a ruler and has servants. This faculty is the one through which will comes about; for will is an appetition toward what has been apprehended, or away from it, whether by sense, by imagination, or by the rational faculty, together with a judgement about it that it should be taken or left.

Appetition may be toward knowing something, or toward doing something, either with the whole body or with some organ of it. Appetition comes about only through the ruling appetitive faculty, while actions by the body come about through faculties that serve the appetitive faculty; these are dispersed in organs prepared for those actions to come about through them. Some of them are nerves, and some are muscles running through the organs by which come about the actions toward which animal and man have appetition. Those organs are such as the two hands, the two feet, and the other organs that can be moved by will. These faculties in organs such as these are all bodily instruments, serving the ruling appetitive faculties in the heart.

Knowledge of a thing may come through the rational faculty, or through the imaginative, or through sensation. When appetition is toward knowing something whose nature is to be apprehended by the rational faculty, the action by which what is longed for is attained is a certain other faculty within the rational faculty, namely the cogitative faculty, through which come thought, deliberation, reflection and inference. When appetition is toward knowing something apprehended by sensation, that by which it is attained is an action compounded of a bodily action and a psychic action, as with a thing we long to see: this comes about by raising the eyelids and by turning our eyes to face the thing we long to see. If the thing is far off, we walk toward it; if there is a barrier before it, we remove that barrier with our hands. All these are bodily actions, while the sensing itself is a psychic action. And so likewise with the other senses.

When one longs to imagine something, this is attained in several ways. One is an action of the imaginative faculty, such as imagining a thing that is hoped for and expected, or imagining something past, or wishing for something that the imaginative faculty composes. The second is what comes to the imaginative faculty from the sensation of something, so that it comes to imagine something about it, that it is to be feared or hoped for; or what comes to it from the action of the rational faculty. These, then, are the faculties of the soul.

parts.name: XXI. On How These Faculties and Parts Become One Soul

lines.text: XXI. On How These Faculties and Parts Become One Soul

The ruling nutritive faculty is something like matter for the ruling sensory faculty, and the sensory is a form in the nutritive. The ruling sensory faculty is something like matter for the imaginative, and the imaginative is a form in the ruling sensory. The ruling imaginative faculty is matter for the ruling rational faculty, and the rational is a form in the imaginative and is not matter for any other faculties; it is thus the form of every form that preceded it. As for the appetitive faculty, it follows upon the ruling sensory, the imaginative and the rational, in the way that heat in fire follows upon that by which fire is constituted as a substance.

The heart, then, is the ruling organ which no other organ of the body rules. Next to it is the brain, for it too is a ruling organ, but its rule is not primary rule; it is secondary rule. For it is ruled by the heart and rules the other organs: it serves the heart in its own person, and the other organs serve it according to what is by nature the heart's purpose. This is like the steward of a man's house: he serves the man in his own person, and the rest of the household serve him according to what is the man's purpose, in both respects. It is as if he succeeds him, stands in his place, deputises for him, and acts for him in what the ruler cannot attend to himself. It is the brain that has charge of serving the heart in the noble ones among its actions.

Among these: the heart is the source of the innate heat. From it the heat spreads into the other organs, and from it they draw their supply, through what spreads into them from it of the innate animal spirit in the pulsing vessels; and through the heat with which the heart supplies them the innate heat is kept preserved in the organs. The brain is what tempers the heat that is to pass to it from the heart, so that the heat that reaches each organ is tempered and suited to it. This is the first of the brain's actions, and the first and most general service it renders to the organs.

Among these, too: the nerves are of two kinds. One kind are instruments for the subsidiaries of the ruling sensory faculty in the heart, so that each of them senses the sensation peculiar to it; the other are instruments of the organs that serve the appetitive faculty in the heart, through which they are able to move with voluntary motion. The brain serves the heart by supplying the nerves of sense with what preserves their powers, by which the subsidiaries are able to sense, keeping these powers intact for them. The brain also serves the heart by supplying the nerves of voluntary motion with what preserves their powers, by which the instrumental organs are able to perform the voluntary motion with which they serve the appetitive faculty in the heart.

For many of these nerves have their roots, from which they draw what preserves their powers, in the brain itself, and many of them have their roots in the spinal cord, which runs on from it; the spinal cord is joined at its top to the brain, so that the brain supplies them with the spinal cord sharing with it in the supply.

Among these, too: the imagining of the imaginative faculty takes place only when the heat of the heart is of a definite measure; likewise the thinking of the rational faculty takes place only when its heat is of a certain kind of measure; and likewise its retaining and recollecting of a thing.

So the brain also serves the heart by bringing its heat to the balance at which its imagining is good, to the balance at which its thinking and deliberation are good, and to the balance at which its retention and recollection are good. With one part of itself it tempers what makes imagining sound, with another part what makes thinking sound, and with a third part what makes retention and recollection sound.

This is because the heart, being the source of the innate heat, could not have the heat in it made anything but strong and excessive, so that there might be a surplus of it to overflow into the other organs, and so that it should not fall short; and it was not so in itself except for an end in the heart.
