This being so, its heat that passes to the organs had to be tempered, while its heat in itself is not at the balance at which its own proper actions are good. For this reason the brain was made by nature cold and moist, even to the touch, relative to the other organs, and a psychic power was placed in it by which the heat of the heart is brought to a definite, determined balance.

The nerves of sense and of motion, being earthy by nature and quick to take on dryness, needed to remain moist, with a suppleness that lends itself to stretching and contracting. The nerves of sense needed, in addition, the innate spirit in which there is nothing smoky at all; and the innate spirit that travels through the parts of the brain is of this condition.

Since the heart is excessively hot and fiery, the roots of these nerves, through which they draw the supply that preserves their powers, were not placed in the heart, lest dryness come quickly upon them so that they dissolve and their powers and actions fail. Their roots were placed in the brain and in the spinal cord, since these two are very moist, so that from each of them a moisture might pass into the nerves that keeps them supple and by which their psychic powers are preserved.

Some nerves need the moisture that passes into them to be watery and fine, with no viscosity at all, and others need some viscosity in it. Those that need a fine wateriness without viscosity had their roots placed in the brain; those that need, in addition, that their moisture be viscous had their roots placed in the spinal cord; and those that need their moisture to be scant had their roots placed at the bottom of the vertebral column and in the coccyx.

After the brain comes the liver, after it the spleen, and after that the organs of generation. Every faculty in an organ whose nature is to perform a bodily action, by which some body separates from that organ and passes to another, necessarily requires either that the other be joined to the first, as many nerves are joined to the brain and many to the spinal cord, or that it have a path and channel joined to that organ, in which that body runs; and that faculty is either serving it or ruling it, as with the mouth, the lung, the kidney, the liver, the spleen and others. And whenever a faculty needs, or it is its nature, to perform a psychic action upon another, it then follows necessarily that there be a bodily channel between the two, as with the action of the brain upon the heart. The first of the organs to be formed is the heart, then the brain, then the liver, then the spleen, and then the other organs follow them.
XXIb. The Organs of Generation

The organs of generation are the last of them all in their action, and their rule in the body is slight, as appears from the action of the two testicles and their preserving the male heat and the male spirit that flow down from the heart in the male animal that has testicles.

The faculty by which generation comes about is partly ruling and partly serving. The ruling part is in the heart, and the serving part in the organs of generation. The faculty by which generation comes about is twofold: one prepares the matter from which the animal that has this faculty comes to be; the other gives the form of that species of animal and moves the matter until there comes to it the form that belongs to that species. The faculty that prepares the matter is the faculty of the female, and the one that gives the form is the faculty of the male.

For the female is female by the faculty by which she prepares the matter, and the male is male by the faculty that gives that matter the form of the species to which that faculty belongs. The organ that serves the heart in giving the matter of the animal is the womb; and what serves it in giving the form, whether in man or in other animals, is the organ that produces the semen. For when the semen reaches the womb of the female and meets there blood that the womb has prepared to receive the form of a human being, the semen gives that blood a power by which it moves until there arise from that blood the organs of a human being and the form of each organ, and in short the form of a human being. The blood prepared in the womb is the matter of the human being, and the semen is what moves that matter until the form arises in it.

The semen stands to the blood prepared in the womb as rennet stands to the milk that curdles from it. Just as rennet is the agent of the curdling in the milk, yet is neither a part of what curdles nor its matter, so the semen is neither a part of what curdles in the womb nor its matter.

The embryo comes to be from the semen as curds come to be from rennet, and it comes to be from the blood of the womb as curds come to be from fresh milk, and a ewer from copper. What produces the semen in the human being are the vessels in which the semen is found, namely the veins beneath the skin of the pubes, the two testicles lending them some assistance in this. These veins open into the channel in the penis, so that the semen flows from those veins into the channel of the penis and runs along that channel until it is poured into the womb, and gives the blood there the beginning of a power by which it changes until the organs arise from it, with the form of each organ and the form of the whole body.

The semen is an instrument of the male. Of instruments, some are joined to the one who uses them and some are separate from him, as with the physician. The hand is an instrument of the physician with which he treats; the lancet is an instrument of his with which he treats; and the medicine is an instrument of his with which he treats. The medicine is a separate instrument: the physician is joined to it only while he makes it, prepares it and gives it a power by which it moves the body of the sick person toward health. When that power has arisen in it, he puts it into the inside of the sick person's body, for example, and it moves his body toward health while the physician who put it there is absent, or dead, for example. Such, likewise, is the standing of the semen.

The lancet does its work only through being joined to the physician who uses it, and the hand is more closely joined to him than the lancet. The medicine, however, acts by the power that is in it without the physician being joined to it. So too the semen: it is an instrument of the male generative faculty, and it acts while separate. The vessels of the semen and the two testicles are instruments of generation joined to the body.

The veins that are the instruments of the semen stand to the ruling faculty in the heart as the physician's hand, with which he works the medicine and gives it a moving power by which it brings the sick person's body to health. For those veins, which the heart uses by nature, are instruments for the semen's being given the power by which it moves the blood prepared in the womb toward the form of that species of animal. When the blood has received from the semen the power by which it moves toward the form, the first thing to be formed is the heart; and once it is formed, the formation of the other organs waits upon whatever faculties happen to arise in the heart.

If there arises in it, together with the nutritive faculty, the faculty by which matter is prepared, the other organs are formed as the organs of a female; if there arises in it the faculty that gives the form, the other organs are formed as the organs of a male. From the former arise the generative organs of the female, and from the latter the generative organs of the male. Then the remaining faculties of the soul arise in the female after the pattern in which they are in the male.

These two faculties, the male and the female, are separated in man into two individuals; but in many plants they are completely joined in one individual, as in many plants that come from seed. The plant gives the matter, which is the seed, and with it gives at the same time a power by which it moves toward the form; for in the seed there is a readiness to receive the form and a power by which it moves toward the form. What gave it the readiness to receive the form is the female faculty, and what gave it a principle by which it moves toward the form is the male faculty. Among animals too there are some whose course is of this kind. And there are also some in which the female faculty is complete, and joined to it is a deficient male faculty which does its work up to a certain extent and then gives out, so that it needs a helper from outside: such as the animal that lays wind-eggs, and such as many kinds of fish, which lay their eggs and leave them, and their males follow them and cast a moisture on them; any egg touched by some of that moisture yields an animal, and any not touched by it spoils.

With man it is not so. Rather, these two faculties are distinct in two individuals, each of whom has organs peculiar to it, namely the well-known organs; the other organs are common to both. Likewise they share all the faculties of the soul except these two. Of the organs they share, those in the male are hotter; and those of them whose action is motion and moving are stronger in the male in motion and in moving.

As for the affections of the soul: those of them that incline toward strength, such as anger and harshness, are weaker in the female and stronger in the male; and those of the affections that incline toward weakness, such as tenderness and compassion, are stronger in the female. Yet nothing prevents there being among human males one in whom the affections are like those in females, and among females one in whom they are like those in males. In these respects females and males differ in man; but in the sensory faculty, the imaginative and the rational they do not differ.

From external things there arise the impressions of the sensibles in the sensory faculties that are subsidiaries. Then the sensibles of different genera, apprehended by the various kinds of the five senses, are gathered in the ruling sensory faculty; and from the sensibles present in these faculties there arise the impressions of the imaginables in the imaginative faculty. There they remain preserved after they have gone from the direct contact of the senses, and it exercises command over them: at times it separates some of them from others, and it combines some with others in many kinds of combination without limit, some false and some true.
XXII. On the rational faculty: how it intellects, and what the cause of that is

It remains after that for the impressions of the kinds of intelligibles to be inscribed in the rational faculty. Of the intelligibles whose nature is to be inscribed in the rational faculty, some are intelligibles that are in their substances intellects in act and intelligibles in act; these are the things free of matter. Others are intelligibles that are not by their substances intelligible in act, such as stones and plants, and in general everything that is a body or is in a body possessing matter, and matter itself, and every thing that subsists through it. For these are neither intellects in act nor intelligibles in act.

As for the human intellect, which comes to a person by nature at the beginning of his existence, it is a certain disposition in a matter prepared to receive the impressions of the intelligibles. So it is in potency an intellect, and a material intellect; and it is also in potency intelligible. The other things that are in matter, or are matter, or possess matter, are not intellects, either in act or in potency; but they are intelligibles in potency and can become intelligibles in act. There is not in their substances what suffices for them to become intelligibles in act of themselves; nor is there in the rational faculty, nor in what nature has given, what suffices for it to become an intellect in act of itself. Rather, in order to become an intellect in act it needs something else that brings it from potency to act. It becomes an intellect in act only when the intelligibles come to be in it; and the intelligibles that are in potency become intelligibles in act when they come to be intellected by the intellect in act. They too need something else that brings them out of potency and makes them be in act.

The agent that brings them from potency to act is a certain essence whose substance is a certain intellect in act, separate from matter. For that intellect gives the material intellect, which is an intellect in potency, something like the light that the sun gives to sight, because it stands to the material intellect as the sun stands to sight. Sight is a faculty and a certain disposition in matter; before anything is seen by it, it is sight in potency, and colours, before they are seen, are visible and seeable in potency.

There is not in the substance of the visual faculty that is in the eye what suffices for it to become sight in act, nor in the substances of colours what suffices for them to become seen and visible in act. Rather, the sun gives sight a light by which it is illuminated, and gives the colours a light by which they are illuminated. Through the light it has acquired from the sun, sight becomes seeing in act and sighted in act; and through that light the colours become seen and visible in act, after they had been seen and visible only in potency.

In the same way this intellect that is in act provides the material intellect with something that it inscribes in it, and that thing stands to the material intellect as light stands to sight. And just as sight, by light itself, sees the light that is the cause of its seeing, and by that very light sees the sun that is the cause of the light, and sees the things that are visible in potency so that they become visible in act, so too the material intellect: by that thing which stands to it as light to sight, it intellects that thing itself; and by it the material intellect intellects the intellect in act that is the cause of that thing's being inscribed in the material intellect; and by it the things that were intelligible in potency become intelligible in act, and the material intellect too becomes an intellect in act after having been an intellect in potency. The action of this separate intellect on the material intellect resembles the action of the sun on sight; for that reason it is called the Active Intellect. Its rank among the separate things that were mentioned, below the First Cause, is the tenth rank. And the material intellect is called the passive intellect.

When there comes to be in the rational faculty, from the Active Intellect, that thing which stands to it as light stands to sight, then out of the sensibles preserved in the imaginative faculty there come to be intelligibles in the rational faculty. These are the first intelligibles, which are common to all people, such as that the whole is greater than the part, and that magnitudes equal to one and the same thing are equal to one another.

The common first intelligibles are of three kinds. One kind is first principles of theoretical geometry. Another kind is first principles by which one comes to know the fine and the base in what it is the nature of a human being to do. Another kind is first principles used to know the states of the existents that it is not the nature of human beings to make, together with their principles and their ranks, such as the heavens, the First Cause and the other principles, and what it is the nature of those principles to bring about.
XXIII. On the difference between will and choice, and on happiness

When these intelligibles come to a human being, there arises in him by nature reflection, deliberation, remembrance and a longing for discovery, and an inclination toward some of what he has intellected and a longing for it, and toward some of what he discovers, or else an aversion to it. Inclination toward what one has apprehended is, in general, will. If it arises from sensation or imagination, it is called by the general name, which is 'will'. If it arises from deliberation, or from reasoning in general, it is called 'choice', and this is found in the human being alone. Inclination arising from sensation or imagination is found in the other animals as well. The attainment of the first intelligibles is man's first perfection; and these intelligibles were given to him only so that he might use them to arrive at his final perfection.

That final perfection is happiness. It is that the human soul should reach such perfection in existence that it no longer needs matter for its subsistence: that it should come to be among the things free of bodies and among the substances separate from matter, and remain in that state for ever and always; except that its rank is below the rank of the Active Intellect. It attains this only through certain voluntary actions, some of them actions of thought and some of them bodily actions,

and not by just any actions, but by certain definite and measured actions that proceed from certain definite and measured dispositions and states of character. For among voluntary actions there are some that hinder happiness.

Happiness is the good sought for its own sake. It is never sought, at any time, in order to obtain something else through it, and there is nothing beyond it, greater than it, that a human being could obtain. The voluntary actions that are useful for reaching happiness are the fine actions; and the dispositions and states of character from which these actions proceed are the virtues. These are goods not for their own sake; they are goods only for the sake of happiness. The actions that hinder happiness are the evils, namely the base actions; and the dispositions and states of character from which these actions come are the deficiencies, the vices and the base traits.
XXIIIa. The faculties and their service

The nutritive faculty in the human being was made only to serve the body; the sensory and the imaginative faculties were made to serve the body and to serve the rational faculty. The service of these three to the body goes back to the service of the rational faculty, since the rational faculty subsists in the first place through the body. The rational faculty is partly practical and partly theoretical. The practical was made to serve the theoretical; the theoretical was made not to serve anything else, but so that through it one may arrive at happiness. All of these are joined to the appetitive faculty. The appetitive faculty serves the sensory, serves the imaginative and serves the rational; and the serving, apprehending faculties cannot fully perform their service and their work except through the appetitive faculty. For sensation, imagination and deliberation are not sufficient for acting unless there is joined to them a longing for what has been sensed, imagined, or deliberated upon and known; for will is to incline, by the appetitive faculty, toward what has been apprehended.

So when happiness is known by the theoretical faculty and set up as a goal, and is longed for by the appetitive faculty, and the deliberative faculty discovers what ought to be done to attain it with the help of the imaginative faculty and the senses, and then those actions are done by the instruments of the appetitive faculty, the actions of the human being are all good and fine. But when happiness is not known, or is known but not set up as a goal that is longed for, and instead something else is set up as the goal and is longed for by the appetitive faculty, and the deliberative faculty discovers what ought to be done to attain it with the help of the senses and the imagination, and then those actions are done by the instruments of the appetitive faculty, the actions of that human being are all not fine.

parts.name: XXIV. On the cause of dreams

lines.text: XXIV. On the cause of dreams

The imaginative faculty is intermediate between the sensory and the rational faculty. When the subsidiaries of the sensory faculty are all sensing in act and performing their actions, the imaginative faculty is acted upon by them, occupied with the sensibles that the senses bring to it and inscribe in it. It is also occupied with serving the rational faculty and with supplying the appetitive faculty.

But when the sensory, the appetitive and the rational faculties are in their first perfections, so that they are not performing their actions, as happens in the state of sleep, the imaginative faculty is left on its own, free of the impressions of sensibles that the senses continually renew in it, and released from the service of the rational and the appetitive faculties. It then turns to the impressions of sensibles that it finds preserved and remaining with it, and works on them by combining some with others and separating some from others. Besides preserving the impressions of sensibles and combining them with one another, it has a third action, which is imitation; for it alone among all the faculties of the soul has the power to imitate the sensible things that remain preserved in it.

Sometimes it imitates the sensibles of the five senses by combining the preserved sensibles that imitate them; sometimes it imitates the intelligibles; sometimes it imitates the nutritive faculty; and sometimes it imitates the appetitive faculty. It also imitates the temperament in which it finds the body. When it finds the body's temperament moist, it imitates moistness by combining the sensibles that imitate moistness, such as waters and swimming in them; when the body's temperament is dry, it imitates the dryness of the body by the sensibles whose nature is to imitate dryness. In the same way it imitates the heat and the coldness of the body, if at some time it happens that its temperament is hot or cold.

Since this faculty is a disposition and a form in the body, it is possible that, when the body is in some temperament, the body should produce that temperament in it. But since it is a psychic faculty, its reception of the temperament that the body produces in it is according to what it is in its own nature to receive, not according to the way it is in the nature of bodies to receive temperaments. For when a moist body produces moistness in some body, the body acted upon receives the moistness and becomes moist like the first. But when moistness acts on this faculty, or moistness is brought near to it, it does not become moist; rather it receives that moistness by the sensibles that imitate it. In the same way, when the rational faculty receives moistness, it receives only the quiddity of moistness, by intellecting it, and not moistness itself. So too this faculty: when something acts on it, it receives that from the agent according to what it is in its substance and its preparedness to receive.

Whatever thing acts on it, if it is in its substance to receive that thing, and if moreover it is in its substance to receive it as it was presented to it, it receives it in two ways: one, by receiving it as it is and as it was presented to it; the other, by imitating that thing by the sensibles whose nature is to imitate it. And if it is in its substance to receive the thing as it is, it receives it by imitating that thing by such sensibles as it happens to find with it whose nature is to imitate that thing; for it does not belong to it to receive intelligibles as intelligibles. When the rational faculty gives it the intelligibles that have come to be with it, it does not receive them as they are in the rational faculty, but imitates them by the sensibles that imitate them. And when the body gives it the temperament that it happens to have at some time, it receives that temperament by such sensibles as happen to be with it whose nature is to imitate that temperament.

When it is given something whose nature is to be sensed, it sometimes receives it as it was given, and sometimes imitates that sensible by other sensibles that imitate it. And when it finds the appetitive faculty in a proximate preparedness for some quality, such as anger or desire, or for certain actions in general, it imitates the appetitive faculty, and the actions are set in motion whose nature is to proceed from that state which is found in the appetitive faculty, prepared at that time to receive them. In such a case the subsidiary faculties sometimes rouse the serving organs to perform in reality the actions that are usually performed by those organs when those actions are in the appetitive faculty. So by this action the imaginative faculty sometimes resembles one who is jesting, and sometimes resembles a dead man. Nor is it only in this way.

Rather, when the body's temperament is such that some affection in the appetitive faculty usually follows upon it, the imaginative faculty imitates that temperament by the actions of the appetitive faculty that arise from that affection; and this before that affection has come about, so that the organs in which the faculty serving the appetitive faculty resides rise up toward those actions in reality. For instance, when the body's temperament becomes one upon which the desire for intercourse usually follows in the appetitive faculty, it imitates that temperament by the acts of intercourse, and the organs of this act rise up in preparation for the act of intercourse, not from a desire present at that time, but because the imaginative faculty imitates the desire by the acts of that desire. And so with the other affections.

So too a person sometimes rises from his sleep and strikes another, or rises and flees, without anything having come upon him from outside; what the imaginative faculty imitates of that thing takes the place of that thing, as if it had occurred in reality. It also imitates the rational faculty, by imitating the intelligibles that have come to be in it by the things whose nature is to imitate intelligibles. It imitates the intelligibles that are in the utmost perfection, such as the First Cause, the things separate from matter, and the heavens, by the most excellent and most perfect sensibles, such as things beautiful to look at; and it imitates deficient intelligibles by the meanest and most deficient sensibles, such as things ugly to look at. And in the same way it imitates those by the other sensibles that are pleasant to look at.
XXIVa. The Active Intellect, the rational faculty and the imaginative faculty

Since the Active Intellect is the cause by which the intelligibles that are in potency become intelligibles in act, and by which what is intellect in potency becomes intellect in act; and since that whose way it is to become an intellect in act is the rational faculty; and since the rational faculty is of two kinds, a theoretical kind and a practical kind, the practical being that whose nature is to do the particulars, present and future, and the theoretical that whose nature is to intellect the intelligibles whose nature is to be known; and since the imaginative faculty is connected with both kinds of the rational faculty:

therefore what the rational faculty receives from the Active Intellect, that thing which stands to it as light stands to sight, sometimes emanates from it upon the imaginative faculty. The Active Intellect then has a certain action on the imaginative faculty: it sometimes gives it the intelligibles whose nature is to come to be in the theoretical rational faculty, and sometimes the sensible particulars whose nature is to come to be in the practical rational faculty. The imaginative faculty receives the intelligibles by the sensibles that it composes to imitate them; and it receives the particulars sometimes by imagining them as they are, and sometimes by imitating them by other sensibles. These particulars are what it is the nature of the practical rational faculty to work out by deliberation.

Some of them are present and some will come to be in the future. But what comes to the imaginative faculty of all these comes without the mediation of deliberation; and for this reason it comes to have, in these things, what after being worked out by deliberation. So from what the Active Intellect gives the imaginative faculty of particulars there come dreams and true visions; and from what it gives it of intelligibles, which it receives by taking their imitations in their place, there come divinations concerning divine things.

All of these may occur in sleep, and they may occur in waking; but those that occur in waking are few, and in the fewest of people. Of those that occur in sleep, most are particulars; intelligibles are few.
XXV. On revelation and the seeing of the angel

That is because, when the imaginative faculty in some human being is very strong and perfect, so that the sensibles that come to it from outside do not take hold of it so as to absorb it entirely, nor does the rational faculty take it wholly into its service, but there remains in it, while it is occupied with these two, a great surplus with which it also performs its own proper actions, and its state when occupied with these two in time of waking is like its state when released from them in time of sleep, then much of what the Active Intellect gives it, the imaginative faculty imagines by imitating it with visible sensibles. Those imagined things then return and are inscribed in the sensory faculty. When their impressions come to be in the common sense, the visual faculty is acted upon by those impressions, and they are inscribed in it. From what is in the visual faculty there come to be impressions of them in the illuminated air that is in contact with sight and traversed by the ray of sight. When those impressions are in the air, what is in the air returns and is inscribed anew in the visual faculty in the eye, and that is reflected back to the common sense and to the imaginative faculty. And because all of these are connected one with another, what the Active Intellect has given of this becomes visible to this human being. When the sensibles by which the imaginative faculty has imitated those things happen to be of the utmost beauty and perfection, the one who sees that says that God has a great and wondrous majesty; and he sees wondrous things, nothing of which can possibly exist among the other existents.

It is not impossible that a human being, when his imaginative faculty reaches the utmost perfection, should receive in his waking from the Active Intellect the present and future particulars, or the sensibles that imitate them, and should receive the imitations of the separate intelligibles and of the other noble existents, and see them. Then, by what he has received of the intelligibles, he has prophecy concerning divine things. This is the most perfect rank to which the imaginative faculty attains, and the most perfect rank that a human being reaches by his imaginative faculty. Below this is the one who sees all of these, some in his waking and some in his sleep, and the one who imagines all these things in his soul but does not see them with his eyes. Below this is the one who sees all of these in his sleep only.

The statements by which these people express are imitative statements, symbols, riddles, substitutions and similes. These people differ from one another greatly. Some receive the particulars and see them in waking only, and do not receive the intelligibles; some receive the intelligibles and see them in waking, and do not receive the particulars; some receive some of them and see them, but not others; some see something in their waking and do not receive some of these in their sleep; some receive nothing in their waking, but receive whatever they receive in their sleep only; receive the particulars in their sleep and do not receive the intelligibles; some receive something of these and something of those; and some receive something of the particulars only, and this is how most are found. People also excel one another in this. All of these are aids to the rational faculty.

Accidents may befall by which a person's temperament changes, so that he becomes prepared by it to receive some of these from the Active Intellect, sometimes in time of waking and sometimes in sleep. In some this remains for a long time; in others it lasts until a certain time and then passes away. Accidents may also befall a person by which his temperament is corrupted and his imaginings are corrupted, so that he sees things of the kind that the imaginative faculty composes in those ways, which have no existence and are not imitations of anything existent. These are the bilious, the mad and their like.
XXVI. On man's need for association and mutual assistance

Every human being is so constituted by nature that, for his subsistence and for reaching the most excellent of his perfections, he needs many things that he cannot provide all by himself alone; rather he needs people, each of whom provides him with something of what he needs. And each one stands to each one in this relation. For that reason a human being cannot attain the perfection for whose sake his natural constitution was given to him except through the associations of many people who assist one another, each providing for each something of what he needs for his subsistence, so that from what the whole community provides, each one gathers everything he needs for his subsistence and for reaching perfection. For this reason human individuals became many and settled in the inhabited part of the earth, and from them human associations arose.

Some of these are perfect and some are not perfect. The perfect are three: great, middle and small. The great is the association of all the communities in the inhabited world; the middle is the association of a nation in a part of the inhabited world; and the small is the association of the people of a city in a part of the dwelling-place of a nation.

The imperfect are the people of a village, the association of the people of a quarter, then the association in a street, then the association in a household; and the smallest of them is the household. The quarter and the village both belong to the people of the city; but the village belongs to the city as its servant, while the quarter belongs to the city as a part of it. The street is a part of the quarter, and the household a part of the street; the city is a part of the dwelling-place of a nation, and the nation is a part of the whole of the people of the inhabited world.

The most excellent good and the utmost perfection are attained first through the city, not through an association less complete than it. Since it is the nature of the good in truth to be attained by choice and will, and likewise evils come about only by will and choice, it is possible for a city to be established for mutual assistance in reaching some ends that are evils.

Therefore every city is one in which happiness can be attained. The city in which association aims at mutual assistance in the things by which happiness is attained in truth is the virtuous city; the association by which people assist one another in attaining happiness is the virtuous association; and the nation all of whose cities assist one another in what leads to happiness is the virtuous nation. Likewise, the virtuous inhabited world comes about only when the nations in it assist one another in reaching happiness.
The virtuous city resembles the complete and healthy body, all of whose organs assist one another to complete the life of the animal and to preserve it in it.

And just as in the body the organs differ and are of unequal excellence in their natural constitution and their faculties, and among them there is one ruling organ, the heart, and organs whose ranks are close to that ruler, in each of which a faculty has been placed by nature by which it performs its action in pursuit of what is by nature the aim of that ruling organ; and other organs have faculties that perform their actions according to the aims of those between which and the ruler there is no intermediary, and these are in the second rank; and other organs perform their actions according to the aim of those that are in this second rank; and so on, until one comes to organs that serve and do not rule at all:

so too the city: its parts differ in natural constitution and are of unequal excellence in their dispositions. In it there is one human being who is the ruler, and others whose ranks are close to the ruler, each of whom has a disposition and a state of character by which he performs an action that follows what that ruler intends; these are the holders of the first ranks. Below these are people who perform actions according to the aims of these, and they are in the second rank. Below these again are those who perform actions according to the aims of these. And so the parts of the city are ranked, until one comes to others who perform their actions according to the aims ; these are the ones who serve and are not served, who are in the lowest of the ranks and are the lowest of all.

But the organs of the body are natural, and their dispositions are natural faculties; whereas the parts of the city, although they are natural, the dispositions and states of character by which they perform their actions for the city are not natural but voluntary. The parts of the city are indeed endowed by nature with natural constitutions of unequal excellence, by which one human being is fit for one thing rather than another; yet they are not parts of the city by the natural constitutions they have alone, but by the voluntary states of character that they acquire, namely the arts and what resembles them. For the counterparts, in the parts of the city, of the faculties that belong by nature to the organs of the body are voluntary states of character and dispositions.
XXVII. On the ruling organ

Just as the ruling organ in the body is by nature the most perfect and most complete of its organs, in itself and in what is proper to it, and has the most excellent share in everything in which another organ shares with it; and below it there are other organs that rule what is below them, their rule being below the rule of the first and under the rule of the first, so that they rule and are ruled: so too the ruler of the city is the most perfect of the parts of the city in what is proper to him, and has the most excellent share in everything he shares with another; and below him are people who are ruled by him and who rule others.

And just as the heart comes to be first, and is then the cause of the coming to be of the other organs of the body, and the cause of their acquiring their faculties and of their being ordered in their ranks, and when one of them is disordered it is the heart that supplies what removes that disorder from it: so too the ruler of this city must come to be first, and then be the cause of the city and its parts coming to be, and the cause of the voluntary states of character belonging to its parts coming about and of their being ordered in their ranks; and if one part of it is disordered, it is he who supplies it with what removes its disorder.

And just as the organs close to the ruling organ perform, of the natural actions that accord with the aim of the first ruler by nature, those that are noblest, and the organs below them perform actions lower than that in nobility, until one comes to the organs that perform the meanest of actions: so too the parts that are close in rule to the ruler of the city perform the noblest of the voluntary actions, and those below them perform what is lower than that in nobility, until one comes to the parts that perform the meanest of actions.

The meanness of actions is sometimes due to the meanness of their subject matter, even though the actions are of great use, like the action of the bladder and the action of the lower intestines in the body; sometimes it is due to their little use; and sometimes it is because they are very easy. So it is in the city; and so it is with every whole whose parts are by nature combined, ordered and bound together: it has a ruler whose relation to the other parts is this relation.

This is also the condition of the existents. For the relation of the First Cause to the other existents is like the relation of the king of the virtuous city to its other parts. The things free of matter are close to the First; below them are the heavenly bodies, and below the heavenly bodies the material bodies. All of these follow the example of the First Cause, aim at it and pursue it, and every existent does this according to its power. But they pursue the aim in ranks: the lowest pursues the aim of what is a little above it, and that pursues the aim of what is above it, and likewise the third has as its aim what is above it, until one comes to those between which and the First there is no intermediary at all. In this order all the existents pursue the aim of the First Cause. Those that were given from the outset everything by which they exist have been made from the outset to follow the example and intention of the First, and so they have come to be in the high ranks. Those that were not given from the outset everything by which they exist have been given a power by which they move toward what they may expect to attain, and in this they pursue what is the aim of the First.
So too must the virtuous city be: all its parts must, in their actions, follow the example of the intention of its first ruler, according to their order.
XXVIIb. Rulership and the intellect

The ruler of the virtuous city cannot be just any human being, because rulership comes about through two things: first, that he be prepared for it by inborn constitution and nature; second, by a voluntary disposition and state of character. As for the rulership that falls to one who is by nature prepared for it: not every art is one by which one can rule; rather most arts are arts by which one serves in the city, and most natural constitutions are constitutions for service. Among the arts there are arts by which one rules and by which one also serves other arts; and among them there are arts by which one only serves and does not rule at all.

So too the art of ruling the virtuous city cannot be just any art whatever, nor just any state of character whatever. For just as the first ruler in a genus cannot be ruled by anything of that genus, as with the ruler of the organs, which is the one over which no other organ can be ruler, and so with every ruler in general: so the first ruler of the virtuous city must have an art that cannot be used to serve at all, and that no other art can rule at all; rather his art must be an art toward whose aim all the arts tend, an aim intended in all the actions of the virtuous city.

That human being must be a human being whom no human being rules at all. Such a human being is one who has been perfected and has become intellect and intelligible in act; whose imaginative faculty has been perfected by nature to the utmost perfection in the way we have described; in whom this faculty is prepared by nature to receive from the Active Intellect, either in time of waking or in time of sleep, the particulars, either in themselves or by what imitates them, and then the intelligibles by what imitates them; and whose passive intellect has been perfected by all the intelligibles, so that nothing of them remains hidden from him, and has become an intellect in act.

For any human being whose passive intellect has been perfected by all the intelligibles has become intellect in act and intelligible in act, and what is intellected of him has become that which intellects. There then comes to him a certain intellect in act whose rank is above the passive intellect, more complete, more separate from matter and closer to the Active Intellect. It is called the acquired intellect, and it becomes intermediate between the passive intellect and the Active Intellect, with nothing else between it and the Active Intellect. So the passive intellect is like matter and substrate for the acquired intellect, and the acquired intellect is like matter and substrate for the Active Intellect; and the rational faculty, which is a natural disposition, is a matter that serves as substrate for the passive intellect, which is an intellect in act.

The first rank by which a human being is a human being is that there should come to be in him the natural disposition that is receptive and prepared to become an intellect in act; and this is common to all. Between it and the Active Intellect there are two ranks: that the passive intellect should come to be in act, and that the acquired intellect should come to be. So between this human being, who has reached this point from the first rank of humanity, and the Active Intellect there are two ranks.

When the perfected passive intellect and the natural disposition are made one thing, in the way that what is composed of matter and form is one thing, and when this human being is taken as having a human form, namely the passive intellect that has come to be in act, then between him and the Active Intellect there is only one rank. And when the natural disposition is made the matter of the passive intellect that has become an intellect in act, and the passive intellect the matter of the acquired, and the acquired the matter of the Active Intellect, and the whole of this is taken as one thing, then this human being is the human being in whom the Active Intellect has come to dwell.

When this comes about in both parts of his rational faculty, the theoretical and the practical, and then in his imaginative faculty, this human being is the one who receives revelation; and God, mighty and majestic, gives him revelation through the mediation of the Active Intellect. What emanates from God, blessed and exalted, to the Active Intellect, the Active Intellect makes emanate to his passive intellect through the mediation of the acquired intellect, and then to his imaginative faculty. By what emanates from it to his passive intellect he is a wise man, a philosopher, and one perfect in intellection; and by what emanates from it to his imaginative faculty he is a prophet, warning of what will be and telling of the particulars that are now, through an existence in which he intellects the divine.

This human being is in the most perfect rank of humanity and in the highest degree of happiness; his soul is perfect, united with the Active Intellect in the way we have described. This human being is the one who knows every action by which happiness can be reached. This is the first condition of the ruler. Then, besides that, he must have the power, by his tongue, to represent well in speech everything that he knows, and the power to guide well to happiness and to the actions by which happiness is reached; and, besides that, he must have sound firmness of body for carrying out the actions concerned with particulars.

parts.name: XXVIII. On the Qualities of the Ruler of the Virtuous City

lines.text: XXVIII. On the Qualities of the Ruler of the Virtuous City

This, then, is the ruler over whom no other human being rules at all. He is the imam; he is the first ruler of the virtuous city, the ruler of the virtuous nation, and the ruler of the whole inhabited part of the earth. This condition can belong only to one in whom twelve qualities are united by nature, qualities with which he was innately endowed.

The first is that he be complete in his organs, their powers well suited to the organs for the actions that are theirs to perform, so that whenever he sets about an action with one of his organs, he accomplishes it with ease.
Next, that he be by nature good at understanding and conceiving everything that is said to him, so that he receives it with his understanding as the speaker intends it and as the matter is in itself.
Next, that he retain well what he understands, what he sees, what he hears and what he perceives; in short, that he scarcely forgets anything.
Next, that he be quick of perception and sharp-witted, so that when he sees the slightest indication of a thing, he perceives it in the way the indication points.
Next, that he be good in expression, his tongue serving him to make plain, completely, everything he has in mind.
Next, that he love instruction and learning and submit to it, receiving it easily, so that the toil of instruction does not pain him and the exertion it brings him does not trouble him.
Next, that he not be greedy for food, drink and sexual intercourse; that he by nature avoid play and hate the pleasures that arise from these things.
Next, that he love truthfulness and those who are truthful, and hate falsehood and those who are false.
Next, that he be great of soul and a lover of honour; that his soul by nature be too great for everything disgraceful, and that his soul by nature rise to what is highest.
Next, that dirham and dinar and the other goods of this world be of little account to him.

Next, that he by nature love justice and the just, and hate injustice and oppression and those who practise them; that he give fair measure, both from his own people and from others, and urge it; that he give redress to anyone on whom injustice has fallen; and that he be favourable to everything he sees as good and beautiful.
Next, that he be just, not hard to lead, neither refractory nor obstinate when he is called to justice, but hard to lead when he is called to injustice and to what is base.
Next, that he be strong in resolve upon what he sees ought to be done, bold and daring in it, neither fearful nor weak of soul.

The union of all these in a single human being is difficult; for that reason one who is born with this nature is found only one at a time, and he is among the rarest of men. If such a one is found in the virtuous city, and after he has grown up those six conditions mentioned before are present in him, or five of them, apart from the prophetic warning that comes by way of the imaginative faculty, he is the ruler. If it happens that no one like him is found at some time, the laws and customs that this ruler and his like laid down, if they have succeeded one another in the city, are taken up and made fixed.

The second ruler, who succeeds the first, is one in whom those conditions have been united from his birth and his boyhood, and in whom, after he has grown up, there are six conditions. The first is that he be wise. The second, that he be learned, preserving the laws, customs and ways of conduct that the first established for the city, following them fully in all his actions. The third, that he be good at deriving in matters for which no law has been preserved from the forebears, and that in what he derives he follow in the footsteps of the first imams. The fourth, that he have good deliberation and the power to derive what needs to be known at any given time concerning present matters and the events that arise, of a kind the first did not deal with, aiming in what he derives at the well-being of the city.
The fifth, that he be good at guiding, by speech, to the laws of the first and to those he has derived after them in which he followed in their footsteps.
The sixth, that he have firmness of body in undertaking the works of war; that is, that he possess the art of war, both the subordinate and the ruling.

If no single human being is found in whom these conditions are united, but two are found, one of them wise and the other possessing the remaining conditions, the two of them are the rulers in this city. If these are scattered among a group, wisdom in one, the second in one, the third in one, the fourth in one, the fifth in one and the sixth in one, and they are in harmony with one another, they are the virtuous rulers. Whenever it happens at some time that wisdom is not part of the rulership, though the other conditions are in it, the virtuous city remains without a king; the ruler who manages the affairs of this city is not a king, and the city is exposed to destruction. And if it does not happen that a wise man is found to be joined to him, the city will not last long before it perishes.
XXIX. On the Opposites of the Virtuous City
The virtuous city is opposed by the ignorant city, the immoral city, the changed city and the erring city. It is opposed also, among individual people, by the weeds of the cities.

The ignorant city is the one whose people have not known happiness, nor has it ever occurred to them; if they are guided to it, they neither take it up nor believe in it. Of good things they know only some of those that are thought, in outward appearance, to be goods, among the things that are thought to be the ends in life: health of body, wealth, the enjoyment of pleasures, being left free to follow one's desire, and being honoured and esteemed. Each of these is happiness for the people of ignorance, and the greatest and most complete happiness is the combination of them all. Their opposites are misery: afflictions of the body, poverty, not enjoying pleasures, not being left free to follow one's desire, and not being honoured.

It is divided into a number of cities. Among them is the necessary city: the one whose people aim at limiting themselves to what is necessary for sustaining their bodies, in food, drink, clothing, dwelling and sexual intercourse, and at cooperating to obtain these.
The city of meanness is the one whose people aim at cooperating to attain wealth and riches, not in order to use wealth for anything else, but because wealth is for them the end in life.

The city of baseness and wretchedness is the one whose people aim at the enjoyment of pleasure in food, drink and sexual intercourse, in short pleasure in what is sensed and imagined, and at preferring jest and play in every way and of every kind.

The city of honour is the one whose people aim at cooperating to become honoured, praised, spoken of and famous among the nations, glorified and esteemed in word and deed, possessed of grandeur and splendour, whether in the eyes of others or among themselves, each according to the measure of his love for this or the measure of what he is able to attain of it.

The city of domination is the one whose people aim at being the conquerors of others and at resisting being conquered by others, their striving being only for the pleasure that comes to them from conquest.
The democratic city is the one whose people aim at being free, each of them doing what he wishes, his desire restrained in nothing at all.

The kings of the ignorant correspond to their cities: each of them manages the city over which he has power only in order to obtain his own desire and inclination. The aims of the ignorant that can be made ends are those we have just enumerated.

The immoral city is the one whose opinions are the virtuous opinions: it knows happiness, God, mighty and glorious, the secondaries, the Active Intellect, and everything that the people of the virtuous city should know and believe; but the actions of its people are the actions of the people of the ignorant cities.

The changed city is the one whose opinions and actions were in former times the opinions and actions of the virtuous city, but it has been changed: other opinions have entered it, and its actions have turned into other actions.

The erring city is the one that believes in a happiness after this life, but has altered this; it holds corrupt opinions about God, mighty and glorious, about the secondaries and about the Active Intellect, opinions that are not sound even if they are taken as representations and imaginings of them. Its first ruler is one who made it appear that he receives revelation without its being so, and in this he has used misrepresentations, deceptions and delusions. The kings of these cities are opposed to the kings of the virtuous cities, their rulerships are opposed to the virtuous rulerships, and so too are all the others in them.
XXIXb. The People of the Virtuous City and Their Souls

The kings of the virtuous cities who succeed one another in different times, one after another, are all as one soul, and as though they were one king who remains for all time. Likewise, if a number of them happen to exist at one time, whether in one city or in many cities, their group is as one king and their souls as one soul.

Likewise the people of each rank in it: when they succeed one another in different times, they are all as one soul that remains for all time. And likewise, if at one time there is a group of people of one rank, whether they are in one city or in many cities, their souls are as one soul, whether that rank is a rank of rule or a rank of service.

The people of the virtuous city have things in common which they know and do, and other things, of knowledge and of action, that belong specifically to each rank and to each one of them. Each one comes within the bounds of happiness only through these two: through what is common to him and to others together, and through what belongs specifically to the people of the rank to which he belongs. When each of them does that, those actions of his give him a good and virtuous disposition of soul; and the more he persists in them, the stronger and more excellent that disposition of his becomes, and its strength and excellence increase. In the same way, persistence in the good actions of the art of writing gives a man excellence in the art of writing; and the more he persists in those actions, the stronger and more excellent becomes the art through which those actions come about, its strength and excellence increasing by the repetition of its actions. The pleasure that follows that disposition of soul becomes greater, the man's delight in himself because of it becomes greater, and his love for it grows stronger.

Such is the state of the actions through which happiness is attained. The more of them there are, the more they are repeated and the more a man persists in them, the stronger, more excellent and more perfect they make the soul whose nature it is to become happy, until it reaches such a bound of perfection that it no longer needs matter and comes to be free of it. Then it does not perish when matter perishes, nor, when it remains, does it need matter.

When it comes to be separate from matter and incorporeal, the accidents that befall bodies insofar as they are bodies are removed from it, so that it cannot be said of it that it moves or that it is at rest. One must then speak of it in the terms that befit what is not a body. Whatever comes into a man's mind of the things by which a body is described insofar as it is a body must be denied of the separate souls, and their state must be understood accordingly; to conceive it is difficult and unaccustomed. Likewise, by their separation from bodies, everything that used to attach to them and befall them is removed from them.

Since among these souls that have separated there are souls that were in different matters, and since it is evident that the dispositions of the soul follow the temperaments of bodies, some more and some less, each disposition of the soul being as the temperament of the body in which it was requires, their dispositions must necessarily differ, because of the difference that was in them. And since the differences of bodies go on without definite limit, the differences of souls also go on without definite limit.
XXX. On the Union of Souls with One Another

When one group passes away, their bodies perishing and their souls set free and made happy, and other people succeed them in their rank after them, take their place and do their actions, then, when these too pass away and are gone, they too come in happiness to the ranks of those who passed before, and each is united with what resembles it in species, quantity and quality. Since they are not bodies, their coming together, however great it grows, does not crowd one another for place, for they are not in places at all; so their meeting and their union with one another are not in the manner found among bodies. And the more the similar separate souls multiply and unite with one another, and this in the manner in which an intelligible unites with an intelligible, the greater and more intense the pleasure of each of them becomes. And whenever those who come after them join them, the pleasure of those who have now joined increases through meeting those who passed before, and the pleasures of those who passed before increase through the union of those who join them; for each soul intellects its own essence and intellects the like of its essence many times over, so that the quality of what it intellects increases.

The increase of those who meet there is like the increase in the power of the art of writing through the writer's persistence in the actions of writing: the joining of one to another, in the increase of each, takes the place of the succession of the writer's actions through which his writing increases in power and excellence. And since those who join one another go on without limit, the increase of the powers and pleasures of each single one goes on without limit through the course of time. Such is the state of every group that passes away.
XXXI. On the Arts and the Kinds of Happiness

The kinds of happiness differ in excellence in three ways: in species, in quantity and in quality. This resembles the way the arts here differ in excellence. Arts differ in excellence in species in that they are arts different in species, one more excellent than another, as weaving and the cloth trade, perfumery and sweeping, dancing and jurisprudence, or wisdom and rhetoric. In these ways the arts whose species differ differ in excellence.

Among practitioners of arts of one species, in quantity is when, for example, of two scribes one has knowledge of more of the parts of the art of writing, and the other has mastered fewer of its parts. For this art is made up of the combination of knowledge of something of language, something of rhetoric, something of good penmanship and something of arithmetic. One of them may have mastered of these, say, good penmanship and something of rhetoric; another, language, something of rhetoric and good penmanship; and another, all four. Difference in excellence in quality is when two have mastered the very same parts of writing, but one of them is stronger in what he has mastered and more knowledgeable. This is difference in excellence in quality.

The kinds of happiness differ in excellence in these ways too. As for the people of the other cities, since their actions are bad, they give them bad dispositions of soul, just as the actions of writing, when they are bad and not as writing ought to be, give a man a bad and defective writing, and the more of those actions he does, the more defective his art becomes. So too the bad actions among the actions of the other cities give their souls bad and defective dispositions, and the more any one of them persists in those actions, the more defective his disposition of soul becomes. Their souls thus become sick, and for that reason they may take pleasure in the dispositions they acquire through those actions. Just as those sick in body, such as many who have fever, because of the corruption of their temperament take pleasure in tastes that are not of a kind to give pleasure, are pained by things that are of a kind to be pleasant, and do not perceive the taste of sweet things that are of a kind to be pleasant, so those sick in soul, through the corruption of their imagination, which they have acquired by will and by habit, take pleasure in bad dispositions and bad actions, and are pained by beautiful and virtuous things, or do not imagine them at all.

And just as among the sick there are some who do not perceive their illness, and some who even think they are healthy, their opinion of this growing so strong that they do not listen at all to what a physician says, so whoever among the sick of soul does not perceive his sickness, and even thinks that he is virtuous and sound of soul, does not listen at all to what a guide, a teacher or a corrector says.
XXXII. On the People of These Cities

As for the people of the ignorant cities, their souls remain unperfected and of necessity need matter for their subsistence, since no true impression of any of the first intelligibles has been traced in them at all. When the matter through which they subsisted perishes, the powers whose nature it was to sustain what has perished perish too, and the powers whose nature it is to sustain what remains remain. If this too perishes and dissolves into something else, what remains becomes a kind of form for that thing into which the remaining matter dissolved. And each time thereafter that this too happens to dissolve into something, what remains becomes a kind of form for that thing into which it dissolved, until it dissolves into the elements; then the last remainder becomes a form of the elements.
After that, its fate depends on what happens to come to be from those parts of the elements into which these dissolved.

If those parts happen to mix in a mixture from which a human being comes to be, it becomes once more a disposition in a human being; and if they happen to mix in a mixture from which another species of animal, or something that is not an animal, comes to be, it becomes once more a form for that thing. These are the ones who perish and pass into nothingness, after the manner of cattle, beasts of prey and vipers.

As for the people of the city: the dispositions of soul which they acquired from the opinions of their forebears free their souls from matter; but the bad dispositions of soul which they acquired from base actions are joined to the first dispositions, trouble them and oppose them. From the opposition of these to those, great pain comes upon the soul; and those dispositions oppose these, so that from those too great pain comes upon these. From the two, two great pains are combined for the soul.

These dispositions acquired from the actions of ignorance are in truth followed by great pain in the rational part of the soul; the rational part does not perceive their pain only because it is occupied with what the senses bring to it. When it is alone, apart from the senses, it perceives the pain that follows these dispositions; and frees it from matter and sets it apart from the senses and from all the things that come upon it from outside. So a man in grief, when the senses bring him what occupies him, is not pained by what grieves him and does not perceive it, until, when he is alone apart from the senses, the pain returns to him.

Likewise a sick man in pain, when he is occupied with things, either suffers less from the pain of the illness or does not perceive the pain at all; and when he is alone, apart from the things that occupy him, he perceives the pain, or the pain returns to him. So too the rational part: as long as it is occupied with what the senses bring to it, it does not perceive the pain of the bad dispositions joined to it, until, when it is completely alone apart from the senses, it perceives the pain, and the pain of these dispositions becomes evident to it. It then remains for all time in great pain. If one of the people of that city who is of his rank is joined to him, the pain of each of them is increased by his companion; for since those who join one another go on without limit, the increases of their pain go on without limit through the course of time. This is the misery opposed to happiness.

As for the people of the erring cities: the one who led them astray and turned them aside from happiness for the sake of one of the aims of the people of ignorance, while he himself knew happiness, is one of the people of the immoral cities; he alone, and not the people of the city, is miserable. The people of the city themselves perish and pass away, after the manner of what the state of the people of ignorance comes to.

As for the people of the changed cities: the one who changed the matter for them and turned them aside, if he is one of the people of the immoral cities, he alone is miserable; the others perish and pass away, like the people of ignorance. So too with everyone who has turned aside from happiness through oversight and error.

As for those of the people of the virtuous city who are compelled and forced into the actions of ignorance: since one who is forced to do something is pained by what he does of it, his persisting in what he was coerced into does not give him a disposition of soul opposed to the virtuous dispositions, such as would trouble that state of his until his standing became the standing of the people of the immoral cities. For that reason the actions he was compelled to do do not harm him. The virtuous man incurs this only when the one who has power over him is one of the people of the cities opposed to the virtuous city, and he is forced to live in the dwellings of those who are opposed to it.
XXXIII. On the Things Common to the People of the Virtuous City
The common things that all the people of the virtuous city ought to know are several. The first is knowledge of the First Cause and of everything by which He is described.

Then the things separate from matter, and what each of them is described by in the attributes and the rank proper to it, until one comes, among the separate things, to the Active Intellect; and the action of each of them.
Then the heavenly substances, and what each of them is described by.

Then the natural bodies beneath them: how they come to be and pass away; and that what takes place among them takes place with firmness, precision, providence, justice and wisdom, and that there is in them no neglect, no deficiency and no injustice in any way at all.
Then the coming-to-be of man, how the powers of the soul arise, and how the Active Intellect pours light upon it so that the first intelligibles, will and choice come about.
Then the first ruler, and how revelation comes about.
Then the rulers who ought to succeed him when he is not present at some time.
Then the virtuous city and its people, and the happiness to which their souls come;
and the cities opposed to it;
and what their souls come to after death, some of them to happiness and some to nothingness.
Then the virtuous nations and the nations opposed to them.

These things are known in one of two ways: either they are impressed in their souls as they exist, or they are impressed in them through correspondence and representation, that is, there arise in their souls likenesses of them that imitate them.

The wise men of the virtuous city are those who know these things through demonstrations and through the insight of their own souls. Those who come next to the wise men know them as they exist through the insight of the wise men, following them, assenting to them and trusting them. The rest of them know them through likenesses that imitate them, because there is no disposition in their minds for understanding them as they exist, whether by nature or by habit.

Both are kinds of knowledge, but that of the wise man is without doubt the more excellent. Of those who know them through likenesses that imitate them, some know them through likenesses close to them, some through likenesses a little more remote, some through likenesses more remote than those, and some through likenesses very remote.

These things are imitated for each nation and for the people of each city through the likenesses that are best known to them, the better known before the less. What is best known may differ among the nations, either for the most part or in some part; so these things are imitated for each nation by things other than those by which they are imitated for another nation.
For this reason there can be virtuous nations and virtuous cities whose religions differ, while they all aim at one and the same happiness and at the very same purposes.
XXXIIIb. Demonstration and Likeness

When these common things are known through their demonstrations, there can be no place in them for contradiction by argument at all, neither by way of sophistry nor for one who understands them badly; for then what the objector contradicts is not the truth of the matter in itself, but the falsehood that he himself has understood in the matter.

But when they are known through the likenesses that imitate them, their likenesses may contain places for contradiction: in some there are fewer places for contradiction and in some more; in some they are more evident and in some more hidden. And it is not impossible that among those who have known those things through imitating likenesses there should be some who light upon the places for contradiction in those likenesses and come to a halt there. These are of several classes.

One class are those who seek guidance. Whenever something appears false to one of these, he is raised to another likeness closer to the truth, in which there is not that contradiction. If he is satisfied with it, he is left there. If that too appears false to him, he is raised to another rank; if he is satisfied with it, he is left there. And whenever a likeness at any rank appears false to him, he is raised above it. If all the likenesses appear false to him and he has in him the capacity to grasp , he is made to know the truth and is placed in the rank of those who follow the wise on their authority. If he is not satisfied with that and longs for wisdom, at the end of it he will know wisdom.

Another class are those who have certain aims of ignorance, such as honour, wealth, pleasure in property and the like, and who see that the laws of the virtuous city forbid them. Such a one sets about the opinions of the virtuous city and seeks to show them all to be false, whether they are likenesses of the truth or what is presented to him of them is the truth itself.

The likenesses he shows to be false in two ways: one through the places for contradiction in them, the other through sophistry and misrepresentation. The truth itself he shows to be false through sophistry and misrepresentation. All this so that nothing may stand in the way of his ignorant and base aim. These ought not to be made parts of the virtuous city.

Another class find all the likenesses false because of the places for contradiction in them; and because, besides, they are of poor understanding, they also go astray from the places of truth in the likenesses, so that even what has no place for contradiction in it at all appears false to them.

When they are raised to the level of the truth so that they may know it, their poor understanding leads them astray from it, so that they imagine the truth other than it is; and they think, further, that what they have conceived is what is claimed to be the truth.

When that proves false to them, they think that what has proved false is the truth that is claimed to be the truth, and not what they themselves understood. Hence it occurs to them that there is no truth at all; that the one who is thought to have been guided to the truth is deluded; and that the one who is said to guide to the truth is a deceiver and an impostor, seeking by what he says leadership or something else.

Some of these are brought by this to perplexity. To others of them it glimmers, as a thing glimmers from afar or as a man imagines something in sleep, that the truth exists, and that it stands apart from the one who would grasp it, for reasons he sees are not within his reach; so he sets about showing false what he has grasped, and does not then count it as truth. Then he knows, or thinks, that he has grasped the truth.
XXXIV. On the Opinions of the People of the Ignorant and Erring Cities
The ignorant and erring cities arise only when religion is built upon certain ancient corrupt opinions.

One of these is that some people said: We see that the existents we observe are opposed to one another, and that each of them seeks the destruction of the other. We see that each of them, when it comes into existence, has been given along with its existence something by which it preserves its existence from destruction; something by which it repels from itself the action of its opposite and guards itself against its opposite; something by which it destroys its opposite and makes from it a body like itself in species; and something by which it is able to make use of all other things for what is useful to its best existence and to the continuance of its existence.

To many of them has been given that by which each overcomes everything that resists it. Each opposite has been put in this state toward every opposite and toward everything other than itself, so that we imagine that each of them is the one intended to be granted, alone and to the exclusion of the others, the best existence. For that reason it has been given everything by which it destroys whatever is harmful to it and of no use to it, and has been given that by which it makes use of whatever is useful to it for its best existence.

For we see many animals spring upon many of the rest and seek to corrupt and destroy them without gaining from this any evident benefit, as though each had been so made by nature that no existent other than itself should be in the world, or as though the existence of everything other than itself were harmful to it, in that it takes the existence of another to be harmful to it even if nothing else came from that other except that it exists.

Further, each of the two, if it does not aim at that, seeks to enslave the other for what benefits it. Every species has been put in this state toward every species, and in many of them every individual toward every individual of its species.

Then these existents have been made to overcome one another and to fight one another. The one that most overpowers the others is the most complete in existence; and the victor always either destroys some, because it is in its nature that the existence of that thing is a deficiency and a harm to its own existence, or makes use of some and enslaves them, because it sees in that thing that its existence is for its own sake. And one sees things proceeding without order, and sees the ranks of existents not preserved.

And one sees things befall each one without its deserving what befalls it in its existence, things that have no existence of their own. This and the like is what appears in the existents that we observe and know.

Then some said after this: This state is the nature of existents, and this is their innate constitution; and what natural bodies do by their natures is what animals that choose ought to do by their choices and their wills, and those that deliberate, by their deliberation.

For that reason they held that cities ought to be overcoming one another and fighting one another, with no ranks among them, no order, and no desert that belongs to one rather than another, whether for honour or for anything else; that each human being should keep to himself alone every good there is for him, seeking to overcome others in every good he obtains; and that the human being who most overpowers everything that opposes him is the happiest. Many of the opinions of ignorance in the cities then arise from these.

Some held that there is no kinship and no bond, neither by nature nor by will; that each human being ought to diminish every other human being, and each one shun every other one; that two should not bind themselves together except under necessity, nor unite except in need; and that their coming together, in whatever they come together for, should be such that one of them is the conqueror and the other the conquered.
