If they are compelled by something coming from outside to come together and unite, this should last only as long as the need, and as long as what comes from outside compels them to it; when it ceases, they ought to shun one another and separate. This is the disease of beasts of prey among human opinions.

Others, when they saw that the solitary man cannot provide everything he needs without having helpers and assistants, each of whom provides him with something of what he needs, held that there should be association. Some of them held that this ought to be by compulsion: that the one who needs helpers should subdue a people and enslave them, then through them subdue others and enslave them too; and that his helper ought not to be his equal, but one subdued by him. For example, the strongest of them in body and arms subdues one man; when that one has been subdued by him, he subdues through him another man or a group; then through those he subdues others, until helpers are gathered to him in due order. When they are gathered to him, he makes them instruments, using them for whatever he desires.

Others held that there is here a bond, mutual love and concord, but they differed over that through which the bond comes about. Some held that sharing in birth from one parent is the bond, and that through it come association, concord, mutual love and mutual support in overcoming others and in resisting being overcome by others.

For separation and mutual aversion come from the difference of fathers; sharing in the more particular and nearer parent requires a stronger bond, and in what is more general a weaker bond, until it reaches such generality and remoteness that the bond is cut off altogether and becomes mutual aversion. Then, in the face of a necessity coming from outside, such as an evil that befalls them, they cannot manage to repel it except by the coming together of many groups.

Some held that the bond is through sharing in procreation: that is, that the male children of this group beget offspring from the female children of those, and the male children of those from the female children of these. That is intermarriage.
Some held that the bond is through sharing in the first ruler, who first gathered them and governed them, so that through him they prevailed and obtained some good among the goods of ignorance.

Some held that the bond is through oaths, alliance and covenant concerning what each human being gives of himself, so that he does not shun the rest nor forsake them, and their hands are one in overcoming others and in warding off from themselves others' overcoming them.

Others held that the bond is through likeness of character and of natural dispositions, and through sharing in language and tongue, and that difference in these makes for separation. This holds for every nation: they ought to be akin among themselves and averse to those other than themselves, for nations differ from one another only by these three.

Others held that the bond is through sharing a dwelling, then sharing in residences; that the most particular is sharing in the dwelling, then sharing in the street, then sharing in the quarter. For that reason they show solidarity with the neighbour, for the neighbour is the one who shares in the street and in the quarter; then comes sharing in the city, then sharing in the region in which the city lies.

There are also things here which it is thought ought to form a partial bond among a small group, among a few, or between two. Among them are long companionship; sharing in food that is eaten and drink that is drunk; sharing in the crafts; sharing in an evil that befalls them, especially when the kind of evil is one and they meet, for each is a consolation to the other; sharing in some pleasure; and sharing in places where one is not safe, each needs the other, as in keeping company on a journey.
XXXV. On Justice

They said: if groups are distinguished from one another by one of these bonds — tribe from tribe, city from city, alliance from alliance, or nation from nation — they are like individuals distinguished one from another; for there is no difference between each individual being distinguished from every other and one group being distinguished from another. After that, they must contend with one another for mastery and fall upon one another. The things over which they contend are safety, honour, wealth and pleasures, and everything by which these are reached. Each group should seek to strip the other of all it has of these and take it for itself, and each stands toward the other in this condition. The group that overcomes the other in this is the one that wins, the one that is envied, and the happy one.

These things are what is in nature, whether in the nature of each human being or in the nature of each group, and they follow from what the natures of natural existents are. What is in nature, then, is what is just.

Justice, then, is mutual conquest, and justice is that whichever of them happens to prevail should subdue the other. The one subdued is either deprived, by being overcome, of the safety of his body, perishing and being destroyed, so that the conqueror alone remains in existence; or he is overcome against his will and remains abased and enslaved: the conquering group enslaves him, and he does what is most useful to the conqueror for obtaining the good over which the victor prevailed, and for keeping it. The enslavement of the conquered by the conqueror is therefore also part of justice, and that the conquered should do what is most useful to the conqueror is also justice. All these together are natural justice, and they are virtue; and these acts are the virtuous acts. When the goods have been obtained by the conquering group, whoever was of greater service in winning those goods should be given more of them, and whoever was of less service, less. If the goods they won were honour, the one of greater service is given more honour; if they were wealth, he is given more; and likewise with the rest. This too, in their view, is natural justice.

They said: as for the other things that are called justice — such as what obtains in buying and selling, the returning of deposits, refraining from taking by force and from oppression, and the like — whoever practises them practises them at first only out of fear and weakness, and under a necessity that comes upon him from outside.

That is, it is as if there were two individuals or two groups, each equal to the other in strength, who take turns in subduing each other. This goes on a long time between them; each suffers bitterly, and they come to a state that they cannot bear. Then they come together and deal fairly with one another, and each cedes to the other some share of what they were contending over, while its marks remain; and each stipulates to the other that he will not try to take away what is in his hands except on conditions, which they agree upon. From this arise the conditions laid down in buying and selling, and, close to them, the honours, then mutual assistance, and other things of that kind.

But this happens only when each is weak in relation to the other and each fears the other. So long as each stands to the other in this state, they should be partners; but when one of them becomes stronger than the other, he should break the condition and seek domination. Or else something comes upon the two of them from outside which there is no way to repel except by partnership and by abandoning mutual conquest, and so they become partners for as long as that lasts. Or each of them has an aim in something he wishes to win, and sees that he cannot reach it except with the other's help and partnership, and so they abandon mutual conquest between them for as long as that lasts, and help one another.

When, for these reasons, a balance has come about among the factions, and time has drawn on in this way, and someone grows up in it who does not know how it first began, he supposes that justice is this which now exists, and does not know that it is fear and weakness; and so he is deceived in what he practises of it. For whoever practises these things is either weak, or afraid that the like of what arises in his own soul — the desire to do it — will befall him from another.
XXXVI. On Humility

As for humility, it consists in saying that a god governs the world; that spiritual beings govern and oversee all actions; in the practice of glorifying the god, of prayers, praises and sanctifications; and in saying that if a man does these things, gives up many of the goods that are longed for in this life, and persists in this, he will be compensated for it and repaid with great goods which he will reach after his death; while if he holds to none of these things and takes the goods in his lifetime, he will be punished for it after his death with great evils that he will meet in the hereafter.

For all these are kinds of tricks and wiles, used against some people and for others. They are tricks and snares for one who is unable to win these goods by assault and open force; a wile with which one schemes who has no power to take them openly and to assault with his hands and his weapons without disguise; and an aid to frightening and subduing people, so that they leave all or some of these goods and others may win them.

So it is with one who is unable to take them openly or to win them by conquest. For one who holds to these things is supposed not to be eager for the goods, and good is thought of him; people rely on him, and do not beware of him, guard against him or suspect him. Rather, his aim is hidden, and his way of life is described as godly, so that his dress and outward form are the form of one who wants none of these goods for himself. This becomes a reason for his being honoured, magnified and looked to for every other good; souls submit to him and love him, and do not object to his following his own desire in everything; rather, everything ugly he does seems fine to all. By this he comes to win, over all of them, honours, positions of rule, wealth and pleasures, and to attain the good. These things, then, were instituted only for this.

Just as the hunting of wild beasts is sometimes by force and open attack and sometimes by stealth and cunning, so winning these goods is sometimes by open pursuit and sometimes by stealth; and they are hunted by making a man suppose, outwardly, that one's aim is something other than what one's aim really is, so that he does not beware, guard himself or resist, and one obtains it with ease.

So whoever holds to these things and persists in them, if he does so only in order to reach the thing for whose sake they were instituted — that is, outward compliance with them so as to win one or all of those goods — is envied by people and held by them to be a man of certainty, wisdom, knowledge and understanding, and is held in high esteem among them, magnified and praised.

But if he does it for its own sake, and not to obtain these goods by it, he is held by people to be deceived, deluded, wretched, foolish, without intelligence, ignorant of his own interest, contemptible, of no worth, and blameworthy. Yet many people make a show of praising him, in mockery of him; some encourage him in it for their own sake, so that he will not compete with them for any of the goods but will leave them, and they may be left in abundance to the one who encourages him and to others; some praise his way and his creed for fear that one who does not follow his way may strip them of what they have; and still others praise him and envy him because they too are deluded, as he is.

These and the like are the views of ignorance that have fallen into the souls of many people from the things observed in existents. And when they have obtained the goods they won, these must be preserved, kept lasting, supplied and increased; for if this is not done with them, they run out.

Some of them held that they should always, all of them together, seek to conquer others; whenever they have conquered one group, they move on to another. Others hold that they should supply these goods both from themselves and from others, and preserve and manage them: from themselves, as by buying, selling, exchange and the like; from others, by conquest. Others held that they should be increased in both ways together.

Others held to this by dividing themselves into two parts: one part increases those goods and supplies them from among themselves by transactions, and one part conquers others for them. So they become two groups, each alone in charge of one thing, the one of conquest and the other of voluntary transaction. Some of them held that the transacting group among them is their females and the conquering group their males; and when one of them is too weak for conquest, he is placed among those who transact, and if he is fit neither for this nor for that, he is made a supernumerary.

Others held that the transacting group should be other people, besides those whom they conquer and enslave, so that these would be the ones charged, in their own form, with guarding the goods that are won, and with supplying and increasing them.

Others said that mutual conquest among existents takes place only between different species; as for those that fall under a single species, the species is their bond, on account of which they should be at peace with one another. Humanity, then, is the bond for human beings, and they should be at peace with one another through their humanity, and then conquer others in whatever of the other species they can profit from, and leave what they cannot profit from. Whatever is of no use and is harmful, they overcome and do away with; and whatever is not harmful, they leave alone.

They said: if this is so, then the goods that by their nature are acquired by some people from others should be acquired by voluntary transactions, while those that by their nature are acquired and obtained from the other species should be acquired by conquest, since the others have no reason and so cannot engage in voluntary transactions. This, they said, is what is natural for man.

As for the man who conquers, insofar as he conquers he is not natural. Therefore, if there must be here a nation or a group that departs from what is natural for man and seeks to conquer the other groups for goods, the natural nation and group is compelled to have people among them who devote themselves solely to repelling such people, should they come upon them seeking to conquer them, and to conquering them for the right of these people, if those others have seized it. So every group comes to have two powers in it: a power by which it conquers and repels, and a power by which it transacts. The power by which it repels is not one it has as doing this of its own will, but through being compelled to it by what comes upon it from outside. These people hold the contrary of what those others hold: those hold that peace comes only from something arriving from outside, while these hold that conquest comes only from something arriving from outside. From this arises this view which belongs to the peaceful cities.
XXXVII. On the Ignorant Cities

Among the ignorant cities are the necessary city, the city of meanness, the base city, the city of honour, and the democratic city. In the others, apart from the democratic city, the aim of the inhabitants is a single kind of end; the democratic city has many aims, for the aims of all the cities are gathered in it.

As for the conquest and defence to which the peaceful cities are compelled, it lies either in the whole body of them or in one particular group, so that the people of the city are two groups: a group in which there is the power of conquest and defence, and a group in which there is not. By these means they keep lasting the goods that are theirs.

This group among the people of ignorance is sound of soul, while the first are evil of soul, because they hold that conquest is the good, and this in two ways, by open force and by stealth: whoever of them is able to use open force does so, and if he is unable, then he uses deceit, fraud, hypocrisy, false show and sophistry.

Others believed that there is a happiness and a perfection which a man reaches after his death and in the other life, and that there are virtues and acts that are truly virtuous, which he does in order to attain happiness after death by them.

They considered, and found that what they observe in natural existents is something they cannot deny or reject; and they supposed that if they granted that all of it is natural, as it is observed, this would entail what the people of ignorance supposed. So they saw fit to say that the natural existents observed in this condition have another existence, other than the existence observed today; that this existence they have today is not natural to them, but is contrary to that existence which is their natural existence; and that one must aim by will, and work, at abolishing this existence, so that that existence which is the natural perfection may come about. For this existence is the obstacle to perfection, and when it is abolished, perfection comes about after its abolition.

Others hold that existents do have their existence today, but that other things have been joined and mixed with them which have corrupted them, hindered them from their actions, and made many of them other than in their true form; so that, for instance, what is not a man is supposed to be a man, and what is a man not to be a man; what is a man's action is supposed not to be his action, and what is not his action to be his action. Thus man at this time does not do what it is his nature to do, and does what it is not his nature to do; he thinks many things true that are not so, and many things impossible without their being so.

On both views alike, the abolition of this observed existence is thought right, so that that other existence may come about. For man is one of the natural existents, and the existence he now has is not his natural existence; rather, his natural existence is another existence, other than this; this which he now has is contrary to that existence and an obstacle to it; and the existence that man has today is something not natural.

Some held that the joining of the soul to the body is not natural, and that man is the soul; that the body's joining to it corrupts it and alters its actions; that the vices arise from it only because the body is joined to it; that its perfection and virtue is to be freed from the body; that in its happiness it has no need of a body, nor does it need a body in order to attain happiness, nor the things outside the body, such as wealth, neighbours, friends and fellow citizens; and that it is bodily existence that makes necessary the civic associations and all the other external things. Therefore they held that this bodily existence should be cast off.

Others held that the body is natural to man, and held that it is the affections of the soul that are not natural to man, and that the complete virtue by which happiness is attained is the abolition and mortification of the affections.

Some held this of all the affections, such as anger, appetite and the like, because they held that these are the causes of preferring those things that are supposed goods, namely honour, wealth and pleasures; that the preference for conquest comes only through anger and the irascible faculty; and that mutual estrangement and aversion come about through this. Therefore they held that all of them should be abolished. Some held this of appetite, anger and what is akin to them, and that virtue and perfection is their abolition.

Some held this of affections other than these, such as jealousy, avarice and the like. And so some held that what bestows natural existence is other than what bestows the existence we now have, and that the cause from which appetite, anger and the other affections of the soul were produced is contrary to that which bestowed the rational part. On this account some of them posited two contrary agents, like Empedocles; and some made the cause of this the contrariety of the matters, like Parmenides in his exoteric views, and others among the natural philosophers.

There are other views besides these, such as what is related of many of the ancients: “Die by will, and you will live by nature.” For they hold that death is of two kinds, natural death and voluntary death. By voluntary death they mean the abolition of the affections of the soul, appetite and anger; by natural death, the separation of the soul from the body; and by natural life they mean perfection and happiness. This is according to the view of those who held that the affections of the soul, appetite and anger, are in man by compulsion.
The views of the ancients that we have mentioned are corrupt. From them branched other views, from which religions spread in many of the erring cities.

Others, when they observed in the states of natural existents what we recounted at first — that they have different and contrary existences, and exist at one time and not at another — and the rest of what we said, held that the existents that are now sensed or intellected do not have defined substances, and that none of them has a nature proper to it such that its substance is that nature alone and nothing else; rather, the substance of each of them is infinitely many things. Take man, for example: what is understood from this word is something of undefined substance.

Its substance, and what is understood from it, is rather infinitely many things; only, what we have now sensed of its substance is this sensible, and what we have intellected of it is this which we claim to intellect of it today. Yet it may be that it is something other than this intelligible and other than this sensible.

So too with every thing that is not now existent: its substance is not only this which is intellected from its word, but this and something else besides, which we have not sensed or intellected, and which, had it been put in the place of this which now exists, we would have sensed or intellected. But what has come to exist is this.

And if someone does not say that the nature of what is understood from each word is not this which is intellected now but other, infinite things, but says instead that it is this, and that it may be other than this, something we have not intellected, it makes no difference.

For what is admissible and possible, if it is posited as existing, entails nothing impossible. So too with everything of which we hold that nothing other than it is admissible, or nothing other than it is possible: it may be otherwise. And what follows by necessity from multiplying, for example, three by three is not the existence of nine; rather, that is not its substance, but what arises from it might be some other number, or whatever else happens among the other existents that are not numbers, or something else that we have not sensed or intellected. Indeed, there may be infinitely many sensibles and intelligibles that have not yet been sensed or intellected, or have not come to exist so as to be sensed or intellected.

So too with whatever follows from something: it does not follow because the substance of that thing requires it, but because it happened so, and because an agent outside that thing brought the other into being in its presence, or at the time of its coming to be, or upon one of its states. For each existent's having come to be now as it exists is either by chance, or because an agent from outside brought it into existence.

It would have been possible for something other than what we intellect today to have come about in place of what is understood from the word “man”; but that agent willed to make, from among those things he was able to make, this intelligible, so that we sense and understand nothing of it except this one aspect.

This is of the same kind as the view of one who holds that, for anything we intellect today, its contrary and its contradictory may be the truth; except that it has happened to be more firmly settled for us to fix in our imaginings that the true and right is this present one. we hold that what is understood from the word “man” may be something other than what is understood from it today, and infinitely many things, each of which is the nature of this understood essence.

And if those things, together with this present intelligible, were one thing in number, then the intelligible today would not be one thing in number, and what is intellected from the word “man” would be nothing other than this present intelligible. But if they are not one in number but many, differing in their definitions, then the name “man” is said of them by equivocation.

And if, besides, they are among the things that can appear in existence together, they would be like the things of which the name ʿayn is said today, and there would also be things infinite in number existing together.

But if they are among the things that cannot exist together, but succeed one another, then they are contrary, or opposed in general. And if they are opposed, whether infinite or finite, it follows that for everything of which we hold that nothing other than it, nor its contradictory, is admissible, its contradictory, or its contrary, or its opposite in general, may also be true, either in place of it or together with its contrary. From this it follows that no statement that is made is true at all, and that everything that is said is true, and that there is nothing impossible in existence at all.

For if something is posited as the nature of something, it may be other than what is understood from its word today; and the nature of something may be among what we do not know — what it is — among the things that can come to exist and be sensed or intellected and become understood, though it is not intellected by us today.

And that of which we do not now know what it is may be its contrary or its opposite in general; so that what is impossible for us may possibly not be impossible. By this view and what is akin to it, wisdom is abolished, and what is imprinted in souls is made into impossible things held as true; for it makes all things capable of having, in their substance, opposed existences and existences without end in their substances and accidents, and makes nothing impossible at all.
